articles.title: Voters in Brazil head to polls as Lula goes up against Bolsonaro's son
articles.snippet: Flávio Bolsonaro, the son of Brazil's imprisoned ex-president, is challenging Lula, who is seeking a fourth term in office.
articles.full_text:
Voters in Brazil head to polls as Lula goes up against Bolsonaro's son
- Published
Polls have opened in Brazil as people choose their new president in a closely fought run-off election.
The choice is between the 80-year-old incumbent, left-winger Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silva, who is seeking a fourth non-consecutive term in office, and right-wing senator FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, 45.
Bolsonaro is the son of former right-wing president Jair Bolsonaro, who was sentenced to more than 20 years in jail for plotting a coup after losing the last election in 2022.
This is Bolsonaro's election to lose after he came top in the first round of voting on 4 October, which US President Donald Trump called a "very big" victory.
Never before has a candidate who trailed after the first round managed to overturn the deficit and win in the second round.
The younger Bolsonaro appeared at a polling station in Rio de Janeiro early on Sunday morning, telling reporters outside that "time has come for real change".
His supporters were jubilant at his final campaign rallies, confident that he would bring change to Brazil through his promised tough crackdown on organised crime, as well as tax and public spending cuts.
Bolsonaro campaigned on the eve of polls opening in Belo Horizonte, the capital of Minas Gerais, which has been a must-win state for any presidential hopeful since the 1980s.
"The time is almost here," Bolsonaro told supporters in a social media video. "There are only a few hours left before we shape the future of our nation for the next 30 or 40 years."
He has also pledged to release his father, who is currently serving his sentence under house arrest due to ill health.
In Barra de Tijuca, Rio de Janeiro, where Jair Bolsonaro has a home, Bolsonaro supporters rallied in support of him dressed in the national colours.
"Brazil needs change, and FlÃ¡vio is the person that represents that today, after so many years of the Left destroying the economy and the country," one told BBC News.
Another said that what she most liked about FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro was his promise to "end violence in Brazil, end terrorism, narco-trafficking, and to reduce interest rates".
Since Bolsonaro's first-round victory, supporters of Lula have arranged huge rallies in support of him to try to boost turnout after 33 million people did not cast a vote earlier this month.
On Saturday, Lula told a huge crowd on Rio de Janeiro's Copacabana beach that this election was a matter of "sovereignty" and people would choose between the one who kissed the Brazilian flag and the one who kissed the American flag.
Lula's administration has accused the US of interfering in Brazil's election, an allegation Washington has called "baseless".
"We're going to win the election for one simple reason: it's true that the people want change [but] they want to move forward," he said. "They don't want to go backward."
A supporter called Roberta told BBC News: "This movement is to show we have strength. We've woken up, we're coming to the street to make a difference and turn the vote around."
A man wearing Brazil's national yellow and green football shirt said Bolsonaro supporters had "appropriated" the jersey but Lula supporters were taking it back.

Lula and his Workers' Party have cast this election as a "battle for democracy", arguing that Jair Bolsonaro's conviction for coup-plotting was evidence that "Bolsonarismo" constituted a threat to Brazil's democratic institutions.
During Lula's latest term in office, relations with Trump have been rocky.
Lula has insisted that Brazil "does not fit into anyone's backyard", an apparent reference to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe Doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with.
Bolsonaro, on the other hand, argues that working with Washington to combat powerful criminal gangs - which wield immense power in parts of Brazil - will restore the state's sovereignty to gang-controlled areas.
He has also been labelling the Workers' Party as corrupt, reminding voters of the massive financial scandals which plagued the party for years and which have turned many voters against it.
Lula plans to be in SÃ£o Paulo to watch the results on Sunday evening, while Bolsonaro is set to be in the capital, BrasÃlia - which is also where his father is under house arrest.

articles.title: Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
articles.snippet: The Israeli Defense Forces announces restrictions on the movement of Palestinian workers in the run-up to Tuesday's election.
articles.full_text:
Israel to close West Bank crossings on election day as crackdown escalates
- Published
All West Bank land crossings will be closed during Tuesday's election in Israel, the country's military says, and Palestinian workers will be barred from entering all settlements.
The restrictions come amid a crackdown in the occupied West Bank after Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in the territory.
The Israel Defense Forces announced a "ban on the entry and exit of Palestinian workers throughout Judea and Samaria and the Jordan Valley, including industrial zones, as well as the closure of all land crossings" on Tuesday.
It said most workers would also be barred from settlements from Sunday, with the exception of industrial zones and a limited number of other areas.
Before the Hamas-led October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, more than 100,000 Palestinian workers were permitted to enter Israel. Since then only a small fraction have had their permits restored.
Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu announced a major operation on Friday in response to the killing of two Israeli soldiers by two Palestinian gunmen in an attack on a checkpoint. Three other Israeli soldiers were injured, and the gunmen were also killed.
The Israeli military have been demolishing homes and businesses in the city of Hebron, with hundreds of families having been displaced.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said about 2,000 residents had been displaced by the operation, which has led to at least one whole street appearing to have been flattened, according to footage shared online.
Even before the entry and exit bans on workers were announced by the IDF on Sunday, the military had cordoned off the city, heavily restricting the movement of its 200,000 residents.
It is common for Israeli forces to demolish the homes of Palestinians who are suspected of carrying out attacks on Israelis in the West Bank - a practice Israeli rights groups have criticised as collective punishment.
Friday's shooting came during a tense time for the region, just days ahead of Israel's election taking place on Tuesday.
In an interview with Israel's i24 television channel released on Saturday, Netanyahu threatened a "very big surprise" for the Palestinian Authority (PA), which governs parts of the territory.
Hebron Mayor Youssef al-Jaabari said the operation was being "driven by the elections" and that Netanyahu and his ministers were attempting to secure the votes of the far right and the settlers.
On Saturday, thousands gathered in Tel Aviv for a large anti-government demonstration.
The protest was organised by the October Council, a group founded by the families of victims and hostages taken by militants on 7 October 2023, to demand accountability for the failure to prevent the Hamas-led attack.
"Three days before the election, we will hold the culminating event marking three years of struggle to uncover the truth, demand accountability, and establish a state commission of inquiry," the October Council wrote on X ahead of the rally.
The gathering saw the participation of the leaders of the four main opposition parties, including Gadi Eisenkot, the former military chief of staff who is neck and neck with Netanyahu.

articles.title: Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
articles.snippet: The tech billionaire accuses Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using the network for military activity.
articles.full_text:
Musk says SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink connection as service restored
- Published
Elon Musk has said his company SpaceX restricted Ukraine's Starlink internet service, after Ukrainian officials said connectivity issues appeared to have been resolved.
The tech billionaire accused Ukraine of violating its terms of service by using it for military activity - but denied being responsible for a simultaneous issue with its US-run, military-grade counterpart Starshield.
Kyiv has not officially commented on Musk's latest claim but Ukrainian presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov said his post was "very strange".
Musk had earlier denied deliberately throttling Ukraine's connection, which it says hampered its ability to conduct defensive operations for more than a week.
The issue first emerged last week during a broader row between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
Musk's latest comments, and the seeming restoration of the service, came after US President Donald Trump said he had told the Tesla and X owner to "put it back", having repeatedly denied instructing him to limit the service.
"Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be," Musk wrote on X on Saturday.
"Ukraine['s] military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week."
He went on to say that SpaceX had "done more to defend Ukraine than any private company on Earth" and reiterated his stipulation that Starshield was a different system and controlled by the US government, adding: "What they decide to do is up to them."
He added in a later post: "[Starlink] can be used for infrastructure that is military, but it cannot be used for unequivocally offensive strikes that make it fair game to be struck back."
Reacting to Musk's post, Beskrestnov said that drones operating via Starlink in Ukraine had a speed restriction of 70-90km/h (43-56mph) and did not work on Russian territory.
"Therefore, we physically cannot use commercial Starlink for deep strikes and medium-range strikes," he wrote on Telegram.
"It is very strange that Elon Musk is not aware of Starlink restrictions in Ukraine."
There was no immediate comment from Ukraine's defence ministry.
Ukraine uses both the civilian service Starlink and the more secure Starshield, depending on what communications are needed, both of which run on networks of low Earth orbit satellites launched by SpaceX.
Starlink allows military units to co-ordinate, particularly in remote areas on the battlefield, while Starshield allows Ukrainian drone operators to see targets in real time, as well as operate interceptor drones.
Russia is not authorised to use Starlink, so when Ukraine sends long-range missiles or drones deep into Russia to hit oil refineries, the network does not work.
Ukraine's Defence Minister Yevhenii Khmara said earlier on Saturday that the military was now recording a "stable connection", with drones now able to reach speeds in excess of 400km/h. Kyiv previously said the connection would cut out above 161km/h.
"The speeds are now where they need to be," Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky wrote on Telegram.
Musk did not disclose in his post why SpaceX had chosen to make the change to its service last week, when Ukraine's extensive use of Starlink had been known for several years.
The connection issues coincided with a tense diplomatic standoff between Zelensky and Trump over Ukrainian strikes on oil infrastructure within Russia.
Trump said the strikes on Russian oil refineries, which Kyiv says are crucial to stemming the main revenue source for Moscow's war effort, have pushed global prices higher.
While the attacks have had an impact on global fuel prices, rises seen this year have primarily been due to the Iran war.
Faced with midterm elections next month and domestic displeasure with rising fuel prices, Trump has waived some sanctions on Russia and agreed a deal with Moscow - criticised by European allies as funding Russia's war machine - to supply Russian diesel to the US and the global market.
Zelensky initially agreed to cease strikes targeting Russian oil facilities on the proviso that Moscow cease striking Ukraine's energy infrastructure, before restarting the strikes after several instances of Russia disregarding this.
The Ukrainian leader said that, as well as seemingly limiting Starlink capability in Ukraine, the US had also threatened to withdraw intelligence sharing if the strikes did not stop, something Trump also denied.
Why is Ukraine so reliant on Starlink and can Europe plug the gap?
- Published9 hours ago
Fighting and aerial attacks continued to be exchanged between Russia and Ukraine overnight.
Ukraine's emergency services said three people were killed and 15 others injured, including an 11-year-old girl, in attacks on the Dnipropetrovsk region, in the south east.
Another six people were injured when a Russian drone struck an apartment block in the central city of Vinnytsia, it said.
The Russian defence ministry said on Sunday that it had struck a cargo vessel it claimed was being used to supply the Ukrainian army while it was en route to the Black Sea port of Chornomorsk overnight.
It also said Russian forces hit a logistics centre, a distribution centre and a logistics terminal in the Ukrainian city of Kharkiv.
Ukraine's defence ministry earlier said it struck a facility in the Russian city of Oryol run by a sanctioned heavy machinery manufacturer. Russian authorities said three people were killed in the strike.
Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, with fighting now into its fifth year.

articles.title: Gunmen kill at least 10 villagers and loot shops in north-east Nigeria
articles.snippet: Police are searching for other casualties, with officials warning the actual death toll could rise further.
articles.full_text:
Gunmen kill at least 10 villagers and loot shops in north-east Nigeria
- Published
Unknown gunmen have raided a remote village in the north-eastern Nigerian state of Taraba, killing at least 10 people, looting shops and setting houses ablaze, police say.
There are fears the actual death toll is much higher, with eyewitnesses speaking of 20 lives lost and a non-governmental organisation suggesting a toll of as many as 50.
The gunmen reportedly swooped on the village of Binnari in the Karim Lamido area mounted on motorcycles just after midday Muslim prayers on Friday in a rampage that went on for up to four hours.
Police say they are searching for other casualties in the bush but the authorities were accused by Amnesty International of failing to protect rural communities.
Nigeria continues to face attacks by armed groups across several regions, including the northwest, northeast and central regions.
The country is also battling a jihadist insurgency in its north-east that has lasted nearly two decades, drawing persistent criticism of the government's handling of insecurity.
Following the latest incident, police said they recovered 10 bodies with gunshot wounds after officers responded to a distress call.
The attackers had fled by the time they arrived but they continued to patrol the area to restore calm, they told BBC News on Saturday.
"We were able to disperse the unknown gunmen though there was no casualty on their side and ours because the terrain is difficult and they're used to the terrain," Assistant Superintendent of Police Victor Mshelizah said.
He added that officers were continuing to search the bush nearby for people who might have been killed or wounded, and warned the death toll could still rise.
Community leader Malam Abubakar Saifullahi told news agency AFP that the attackers had arrived on about 50 motorcycles, two men apiece.
"They looted shops and took cash, foodstuffs and other provisions," he said. "They also took motorcycles abandoned by people fleeing the attack."

Survivors who spoke to AFP said they had counted at least 20 dead.
"People were running in different directions to escape the attack," Binnari resident Isiyaku Musa said. "Nobody knew where it was safe to go."
Another survivor, Sa'idu Nuhu, said that some people were still missing.
Amnesty's Nigeria director, Isa Sanusi, told BBC News on Saturday that the NGO had spoken to some of the bereaved families who said up to 50 people had died.
"The initial funeral had 37 people," he said.
Sanusi called for an impartial investigation into the killings, accusing the authorities of leaving rural communities "at the mercy of gunmen that are repeatedly commit atrocities with impunity".

articles.title: More than 1,300 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
articles.snippet: Hundreds of thousands took part in demonstrations in France, with protests also taking place in other European countries.
articles.full_text:
More than 1,300 arrested as clashes follow another day of mass protests across France
- Published
More than 1,300 arrests were made as hundreds of thousands of people took part in another day of protests across France on Saturday that were followed by some clashes later in the day, officials have said.
After largely peaceful demonstrations, police fired tear gas and water cannon to disperse protesters in a number of cities including Paris, while barricades were set alight in Marseille and people ripped boards from a shop in Bordeaux.
Officials have so far managed to avoid rioting and looting on the scale seen last weekend, which resulted in some of the worst scenes of disorder in France's modern history.
The interior ministry said an estimated 410,000 people protested on Saturday, while the unions put the number at about 800,000.
Some 70,000 police officers were deployed and restrictions imposed in several cities to prevent the latest protests over the cost of living and poor school conditions from descending into the kind of chaos which saw officers outnumbered, hundreds of businesses looted and buildings torched.
The interior ministry said 53 officers were hurt in clashes across the country on Saturday.
French President Emmanuel Macron had decreed earlier this week that only demonstrations organised by a recognised trade unions would be permitted. Hundreds of people have been jailed for vandalism, arson and looting after fast-track court hearings.
Clashes between protesters and riot police in Paris erupted at the end of a peaceful march from the city's Porte d'Italie towards Porte de Vincennes, where the police operation included an elite unit that usually deals with organised crime and counter-terrorism.
Some protesters were seen erecting makeshift barricades and pelting officers with projectiles, while police baton-charged groups of masked youths who were smashing the windows of a car dealership.
French Interior Minister Laurent NuÃ±ez said that "several thousand radical activists gathered at the rear of the march, including around 500 individuals identified as rioters", news agency AFP reported.
The Interior Ministry said 142 people were arrested in the French capital on Saturday, less than half of the number arrested on the same day last week.
In the southern port of Marseille, rubbish bins were set ablaze and metal sheets used to block streets. A law enforcement vehicle was seen driving through a burning barricade in France's second-largest city.
Meanwhile, some protesters in dark clothing and face coverings were seen taking boards off a building to build a street barricade in the southern city of Bordeaux.
In Lyon, police used tear gas grenades to disperse a crowd which had reportedly gathered in an area deemed off-limits by the local prefecture.
"There were around 150 of us, mostly secondary school and university students. Then the tear gas came almost immediately. You could barely see anything in the street," said one protester in France's third-largest city.
NuÃ±ez also said two people had been "seriously injured": one in the south-western city of Toulouse and another one in Clermont-Ferrand, central France. He said the number of arrests across the country would likely rise.
The man in Toulouse, a 20-year-old protester, had several fingers torn off one hand when a nearby explosive went off, Franceinfo reported, citing the medic who treated him.
As the unrest continued into the early hours of Sunday morning, authorities in Bouches-du-RhÃ´ne, the region in which Marseilles sits, said seven businesses had been "looted or damaged".
Earlier, a peaceful protester in Paris who gave her name as Zelie told the BBC people had taken to the streets because they were "really frustrated" and had been "suffering a lot" since Macron came to office.
"They keep us quiet. They take our money, they tax us a lot and we can't say anything. Today we are in the streets because it's been too long, it's been too much," the 26-year-old said.
Two masked teenage protesters, who did not want to give their names, also said their generation was in despair and felt abandoned by the government.
"I think looting is really not good," one of the demonstrators said of last Saturday's disorder. "But it's because of poverty and the violence of the police."
He added that the protests would end "when we have a response to our demands. We really want a change in France".
Meanwhile, some 13,000 people joined a rally against the hard-right National Rally (RN) party in the north-central city of OrlÃ©ans, which proceeded peacefully.
The recent unrest has played out against a backdrop of a polarised political landscape, with France preparing for what could be the most divisive election period in a generation.
Macron will leave office next spring and polls suggest French voters will ultimately face a choice between RN's candidate Marine Le Pen and that of the radical-left La France Insoumise (France Unbowed).
Leading figures from both parties have levelled the blame for the disorder at Macron, though right-wing figures have also heaped criticism on rioters while left-wing leaders support the union-led protests.
LFI candidate Jean-Luc MÃ©lenchon said French media had not covered the peaceful protests while police had created "a setup deliberately designed to provoke chaos" that had "mutilated two people".
Mass protests triggered by similar issues as in France also rocked several other European cities on Saturday.
In Barcelona, more than 120 people were arrested after a student protest descended into what local authorities described as "gratuitous violence".
In Albania's capital Tirana, riot police fired tear gas to disperse thousands of anti-government demonstrators, while clashes were also reported in Belgium's capital Brussels.
In Milan, northern Italy, a major security operation including hundreds of soldiers alongside police prevented protesters gathering in the city. Many had feared a repeat of violent scenes last week when some started fires, smashed windows and looted shops.
Around 550,000 people took part in last weekend's demonstrations against rising fuel prices and the cost of living, with frustrations escalating after weeks of student protests. The chaos which followed resulted in more than 2,500 arrests.
Marches were initially largely peaceful but became marred by scenes of violence, looting and destruction, with more than 2,000 shops and other businesses across France said to have been directly impacted. The damage was estimated "at hundreds of millions euros", France's Chambers of Commerce and Industry (CCI) said.
One demonstrator's hand was blown off by a police crowd-control grenade, according to AFP, while about 1,000 police officers were injured.
The French authorities later said they were forced to impose overnight curfews in Paris and other cities.
The continuing protests come ahead of France's presidential elections in six months' time, and leading contenders have levelled the blame at Macron and his ministers.

articles.title: Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
articles.snippet: Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to fight the blaze at the Nazi dictator's Alpine residence in Germany.
articles.full_text:
Man arrested after fire at Hitler's mountaintop Eagle's Nest retreat
- Published
Police in the southern German state of Bavaria have detained a 33-year-old German man during a fire at Adolf Hitler's Alpine mountain retreat, the Kehlsteinhaus, also known as the Eagle's Nest.
Dispatchers in Traunstein received a fire alarm from the building at 21:15 local time (19:15 GMT) on Friday and firefighters found it engulfed in flames.
Some 200 emergency personnel were deployed to the scene where the blaze was still burning early on Saturday, as police said difficult terrain hindered efforts to bring the fire under control.
Police said they apprehended the man riding a motorcycle near the scene, German media reported. A criminal investigation has been launched.
There is currently nothing to suggest the involvement of further suspects, police official Gerhart Holzinger told a press conference on Saturday afternoon.
Public prosecutor Rainer Vietze said a psychiatric report had concluded the 33-year-old man showed signs of possible mental illness and diminished responsibility might therefore be assumed.
Vietze said a possible political motive was also being considered, but stressed the investigation was in its early stages.
The residence, above the town of Berchtesgaden, was one of several buildings in the area used by the Nazi dictator and his entourage during World War Two.
Hitler and top Nazi officials used his nearby Berghof residence to plan the invasion of the USSR in 1941 and the whole complex was considered one of his headquarters.
He also used the area as a backdrop for propaganda films portraying him as a lover of animals and nature.
Local media reported that site had been "largely destroyed" and the public was urged to avoid the area.
Bavaria's Interior Minister Joachim Herrmann told reporters that the site would "under no circumstances remain a ruin", broadcaster BR24 reported. "It is important that we continue our work of remembrance," he added.
Completed by the Nazis in 1938, the Eagle's Nest, which sits at an elevation of around 1,800m (5,900ft), escaped destruction after their defeat in 1945.
Since then, it has become a popular tourist destination and houses a mountain inn.
It serves as "a cautionary reminder of the abysses of the inhumane Nazi dictatorship", according to its official website, external.
During WW2, Hitler and his followers were responsible for the deaths of tens of millions of people, including the mass murder of European Jews. Homosexuals, gypsies, the disabled and ethnic minorities were sent to concentration camps and put to death.
There has been a wider debate in Germany and Vienna over whether to preserve, repurpose or demolish buildings connected to Hitler.
While some say these buildings should be preserved for historical reasons, others have raised concerns that they could be used as monuments or places of pilgrimage for neo-Nazis and far-right extremists.
In June, Berlin authorities announced they would tear down one of Hitler's bunkers - described at the time as "the power centre of Nazi Germany" - to build flats and offices on the site.
Those critical of the plans said the bunker had "significant historical value" and that it should have been turned into a museum and memorial site with an exhibit about the end of the war.
And in July, after years of controversy, Austrian authorities refurbished the house in the town of Braunau am Inn in which Hitler was born and turned it into a police station.

articles.title: Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after revealing diagnosis
articles.snippet: The ex-wife of Donald Trump Jr, with whom she shares five children, announced in May that she had been diagnosed with breast cancer.
articles.full_text:
Vanessa Trump says she is cancer-free six months after revealing diagnosis
- Published
Vanessa Trump, the former wife of Donald Trump Jr, has announced that she is cancer-free following her breast cancer diagnosis earlier this year.
Trump, 48, who has five children with US President Donald Trump's eldest son, said that her recent tests results "came back clear, so I'm finally cancer-free", in a short video on her 19-year-old daughter Kai's Instagram account.
Vanessa and Kai Trump then released a longer video on Saturday, in which they discussed breast cancer awareness, early detection and prevention.
Vanessa Trump separated from Trump Jr in 2018 and announced last year that she had begun dating US pro golfer Tiger Woods.
"October is Breast Cancer Awareness Month, a time to raise awareness about early detection, education, and support for those affected by breast cancer," Kai Trump wrote on Instagram.
"I sat down with my mum and Dr Nicole Saphier to talk about my mum's journey with breast cancer and learn more about prevention and early detection."
Kai's post received over 20,000 likes and hundreds of comments from people offering support and well wishes, including from US singer and media personality Mary Millben.
Vanessa Trump explained in the YouTube video that she experienced arm pain for several months before discovering a pea-sized lump in her breast, which testing confirmed was a cancerous tumour.
"It's a process you have to deal with," she said of the days spent waiting for her test results.
"You have to be mentally strong for yourself because you're going to need the strength to fight whatever challenge it is that's coming towards you."
Trump said she was first diagnosed with breast cancer in April. She publicly announced the diagnosis in May, saying in a social media post that she had undergone surgery and was working on a treatment plan with her medical team.
She eventually had a lumpectomy and radiation treatments, she said.
The average risk of a woman in the US developing breast cancer is about 1 in 8, or 13%, according to the American Cancer Society. The disease also accounts for 30% of all new female cancers every year, it says.
Surgery cures most breast cancers, but if some cancer cells remain, chemotherapy, radiotherapy and endocrine therapy can reduce the long-term risk.
Treatments have been advancing, including more targeted therapies for early breast cancer, new types of hormonal therapies, and more precise and effective radiotherapy.

articles.title: Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban
articles.snippet: The authorities had justified the ban by saying online content was fuelling conflict, while the opposition had condemned it as an abuse of power.
articles.full_text:
Gabon says access to social media restored after eight-month ban
- Published
Gabon says it has lifted a ban on social media imposed eight months ago - a move that triggered widespread criticism at the time.
The High Communication Authority (HAC) announced the U-turn on Saturday in a televised statement. The BBC has approached the country's media regulator for comment.
The ban had been introduced on 17 February, with the HAC saying that online content was fuelling conflict and deepening divisions in the country.
The move came as a shock to the central African nation of about 2.5 million people, where social media platforms such as Facebook, TikTok, YouTube and Instagram have been particularly popular with younger people who use it for business as well as pleasure.
Many turned to VPNs in order to continue accessing social media sites following the ban.
The ban had been imposed at a time when the Gabonese President Brice Oligui Nguema was facing a wave of social unrest less than a year after his election.
Teachers and civil servants had staged strikes over what they said were low pay and poor working conditions.
The opposition said the suspension was an abuse of power.
Nguema won last year's elections with more than 90% of the vote, two years after his coup had ended more than five decades of rule by the Bongo family.
At the time he pledged to reform Gabon, a small, oil- and timber-rich country, where digital blackouts were used by the previous governments to control information.

articles.title: Bangladesh per capita GDP forecast to outstrip India’s: What does it mean?
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Bangladesh expected to surpass India's per capita GDP this year, but that's not the complete economic picture.
articles.full_text:
Bangladesh per capita GDP forecast to outstrip India’s: What does it mean?
Bangladesh is expected to surpass India’s per capita GDP this year, but the complete economic picture is a mix of success stories and new challenges.
Bangladesh’s per capita gross domestic product (GDP) is projected to be higher than that of Asia’s third largest economy, India, this year, according to the International Monetary Fund (IMF).
GDP is a measure of all goods and services produced within a country during a specific period. India’s GDP is nearly eight times larger than Bangladesh’s. But its neighbour’s per capita GDP, which is GDP divided by the total population, is expected to surpass that of India, the world’s most populous nation.
The projected 2026 per capita GDP of Bangladesh, home to about 175 million people, is $2,886, compared with $2,749 in India as Dhaka emerges as one of South Asia’s notable economic success stories over the past two decades. Bangladesh’s economy is currently larger than that of Pakistan, from which Dhaka seceded in 1971.
Experts link the rise to the country’s $38bn garment industry, remittances and growing participation of women in the workforce.
But high inflation and slowing growth are now putting that progress under pressure. Meanwhile, the Indian economy is expected to grow by 7 percent this year, compared with 3.6 percent in Bangladesh.
So how should one read these numbers, and what do they really mean for millions of people living in these countries?
What’s in the IMF report?
The IMF’s October 2026 World Economic Outlook report underscores differences in how the Indian and Bangladeshi economies are reacting to inflation and the economic pressures caused by two major wars that have jolted energy markets.
Bangladesh is expected to have a GDP of $506.4bn in 2026, compared with India’s $4.15 trillion. But its lead in GDP per capita reverses when adjusted for purchasing power parity (PPP), which accounts for differences in local prices. On this measure, India is projected to have a GDP per capita at $12,998, compared with Bangladesh’s $10,884.
PPP is an economic metric that represents what money can actually buy in different countries after adjusting for the cost of living. The figures mean that Indians have a higher buying capacity than Bangladeshis.
The IMF projected India’s average consumer-price inflation at 5 percent, compared with 8.7 percent in Bangladesh, pointing to greater cost-of-living pressures in Dhaka.
India is relatively wealthier than Bangladesh and is home to a big industrial base, including its significant technology sector.
India’s economy is expected to grow by 7 percent in 2026, nearly twice Bangladesh’s 3.6 percent rate.
For context, the average per capita GDP in developing economies is about $7,746 – and the global average is about $15,889 – against Bangladesh’s $2,886 and India’s $2,749.
Where are India’s and Bangladesh’s economies expected to go?
In the next year, the IMF report projected that Bangladesh’s per capita GDP would reach $3,219, still higher than India’s $3,036 – a difference, according to the estimates, that should continue marginally in 2028.
In 2029, based on current growth forecasts, India’s per capita GDP of $3,661 would top Bangladesh’s $3,334, according to the IMF.
Experts noted that Bangladesh is facing a weaker near-term growth outlook, even as its projected GDP per capita edges above India’s.
But GDP per capita alone does not paint a complete economic picture because it conceals inequalities in income and wealth distribution. The dollar-denominated figure also changes with the exchange rate, which means that a change in a currency’s value can alter the relative numbers without a change in economic output.
In brief, the growth in Bangladesh’s economy in the past two decades has focused on export-oriented manufacturing, particularly its ready-made garment industry, which has been a major source of export earnings and employment, in addition to remittances from Bangladeshis working abroad.
Meanwhile, India has a diversified economy, with services playing a major role alongside manufacturing and agriculture. Its domestic market, technology and business services, industrial base and consumer demand provide multiple sources of economic activity.
In both countries, however, economic growth over the past decade has been unequal with increasing concentration in wealthier households.
Is Bangladesh a South Asian success story?
To some extent, yes, analysts said while expressing caution about unequal growth.
Santosh Mehrotra, an Indian economist, told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh’s economy has shown consistent economic growth of 6 percent per annum alongside a long-term decline in population growth.
The country has also seen its manufacturing contribution to gross value added shoot up from 16.6 percent in 2014 to 22 percent in 2025, Mehrotra said. On the other hand, World Bank data showed India’s manufacturing value added falling from 15.1 percent of GDP in 2014 to 13.5 percent in 2024.
“That’s a positive side of export-oriented manufacturing growth that Bangladesh is getting right,” he said.
However, the global energy shock from the United States-Israel war on Iran, which has disrupted maritime traffic in the Strait of Hormuz, has jolted Bangladesh.
Bangladesh imports 95 percent of its oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG), and much of these imports comes from the Middle East.
The ready‑made garment industry, which accounts for more than 80 percent of Bangladesh’s export earnings, has also been hit as its shipment routes via the Red Sea and the Middle East have been disrupted.

articles.title: The search for gold is a dangerous and laborious gamble for Sudan’s miners
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: As Sudan’s war destroys livelihoods, the death of 16-year-old Altayeb Alhadi highlights dangers of artisanal mining.
articles.full_text:
The search for gold is a dangerous and laborious gamble for Sudan’s miners
As Sudan’s war destroys livelihoods and pushes people towards artisanal mining, the death of 16-year-old Altayeb Alhadi highlights the dangers facing young workers in an industry offering little protection.
When Altayeb Alhadi was just six years old, his father died after a well collapsed in his village in White Nile state, south-central Sudan. Two months later, and his mother also died, leaving the five children in the family as orphans. As the eldest of the siblings, it was Altayeb’s responsibility to find work and help the family survive.
At 14, he travelled hundreds of kilometres from his home in Galli village to seek work in the north, where gold mines dot the landscape, so he could feed his siblings and keep them in school.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3At least 72 Sudanese miners killed in air strike: Rights monitor
- list 2 of 3Deadly gold mine air strikes highlight Egypt-Sudan border insecurity
- list 3 of 3Sudan’s soaring fuel prices make getting by harder for workers
“We warned him about the dangers, but he was ambitious. Some relatives were already working in the area although they had found jobs in restaurants and other services rather than underground extraction,” Ayateb’s uncle Alhadi Hamid told Al Jazeera.
The boy initially worked in transport and other jobs, but when he heard lucrative stories from miners in the area, he began to search for gold in the surrounding mountains.
Altayeb died in an air strike attributed to the Egyptian military at a gold-mining site near Jabal Al-Aigdat in Sudan’s Red Sea region on October 10, which killed at least 72 miners, a few months after he began working at the site.
“It was less than 30 minutes since we separated, and he said he was going to the mine. We suddenly heard a loud sound of bombardment, and we ran. It was too chaotic with people running in all directions and many attacks taking place within a few minutes,” a fellow miner told Al Jazeera, speaking on condition of anonymity.
“We found Altayeb with his hand and leg [blown off] and a severe injury to his abdomen [which] was open. We tried to help him and took him to a safer place near a mountain. We were terrified. He died within hours. … We couldn’t believe how quickly things could happen.”
Altayeb worked alongside about 15 young men and children, using basic tools to extract gold from the rocks. The miners worked night and day, taking the material they gathered to nearby mills for processing.
Proceeds from any gold found were shared, but earnings depended on the amount of gold recovered and individual agreements. On productive days, the group could earn more than $100, the miner said.
“We used to dig for two to three weeks until we found a gram or less. If the gold percentage in the well wasn’t good, we would change locations. When we found a gram or less, we sold it and shared the profit, which was about $100,” Altayeb’s former colleague said.
For young people supporting relatives, even irregular earnings in these dangerous gold mines can seem preferable to unemployment.
Altayeb told his siblings 10 days before his death that he would soon return home, his sister Rogaia Alhadi told local media.
Friends told the family that Altayeb visited them at a restaurant near the mining site on the morning of the attack, his uncle said. They shared a cup of tea before heading towards the mine for the final time. Minutes later, the air strike hit the area.
Authorities in Egypt have accused Sudanese miners of crossing its border and reportedly linked some to gold smuggling, drugs and human trafficking. The Sudanese side did not respond to these allegations.
Since a civil war between Sudan’s military and the Rapid Support Forces paramilitary group broke out in 2023, the economy has tanked and forced thousands with no other source of income to find work in the artisanal gold mines of northern Sudan.
This can vary from independent prospecting to working in investor-owned pits for a share of the proceeds. Earnings depend on the amount of gold found, equipment and fuel costs, and profit percentages agreed with financiers.
Although some miners strike gold, they still face an array of dangers, ranging from collapsing shafts and unstable ground to air strikes. Limited medical care makes mining, particularly in remote areas, especially hazardous.
Living conditions are also extremely hard. Mohamed Awadalkarim, who was a miner in River Nile state for 10 years, said workers often shelter in makeshift huts made from burlap sacks and plastic sheeting. Their diet consists mainly of lentils and sorghum porridge.
But for families without reliable incomes, mining offers a possible source of immediate earnings. Miners may spend hours searching for gold and not find enough to cover their expenses. Others share proceeds with investors or equipment owners, leaving them with limited money left.
Artisanal and small-scale mining accounted for 53.71 tonnes, or about 83 per cent, of Sudan’s declared gold production in 2024, but this was just in areas under government control, according to research by the Chatham House think tank. About one million people were involved in artisanal mining across Sudan’s 18 states, generating $1bn annually for the country.
Artisanal mines, while generally viewed as being outside the main war-funding networks, have still been exposed to violence.
On June 16, several people were reportedly killed and injured in attacks on mining sites near the Egyptian border, according to local sources and miners.
The repeated air strikes near Sudan’s border with Egypt have raised concerns about civilian protection, territorial sovereignty and accountability.
Egyptian authorities have accused Sudanese prospectors of crossing the border to mine near a concession managed by an Egyptian company, but there is little independent evidence to back these claims.
Sudanese military leader Abdel Fattah al-Burhan reportedly ordered a fact-finding committee involving prosecutors, judicial representatives and security agencies to investigate the attack. Findings from an inquiry into a similar incident announced in June have not been made public.
Altayeb paid the highest price in this regional conflict and the hunt for gold, which provides huge profits for some and meagre incomes for many.
Altayeb’s siblings are now living with their extended family, including uncles, aunts and cousins. People who know them are trying to help his brothers and sisters and are carrying out community initiatives in Galli to keep his memory alive.
“We will raise the children and care for them as he would have wanted. He was young, caring and brave, and he will always be remembered,” Altayeb said.

articles.title: Saudi air defences intercept Houthi barrage near Mecca

articles.full_text:
Saudi air defences intercept Houthi barrage near Mecca
Yemen’s Houthi rebels launch a barrage of missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia, triggering widespread civil defence alerts and international condemnation.
The Saudi-led coalition has intercepted a barrage of projectiles from Yemen that targeted cities across the kingdom.
Saudi Civil Defence said that shrapnel from two intercepted ballistic missiles, suspected to have been fired by Yemen’s Houthi rebels, fell in Jeddah, Taif, Rabigh, and Wadi Al-Mughammas in Mecca province.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items- list 1 of 3Iran says won’t allow US warships to get close as Trump ponders new attacks
- list 2 of 3Houthis launch attacks on Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Aden
- list 3 of 3Saudi Arabia intercepts missiles and drones as fighting with Houthis rages
A drone and ballistic missile were also intercepted over the Saudi capital Riyadh during the barrage, which began Saturday evening.
By midday Sunday, coalition forces had intercepted a cruise missile targeting Khamis Mushait, with warning sirens blaring out across Taif and Jazan. In total, 10 ballistic missiles directed at the southern region were intercepted.
Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) Secretary-General Jasem Mohamed AlBudaiwi said the strikes represented “a grave violation of the sanctity of the Holy Sites and a provocation to the sentiments of Muslims worldwide”, referring to the interceptions in Mecca, home of the Kaaba and Masjid al-Haram. The Houthis, a Zaydi Shia group, have denied targeting Muslim holy sites in Saudi Arabia.
The kingdom has faced waves of Houthi missile and drone strikes in recent weeks, targeting civilian and military infrastructure.
Riyadh announced late Saturday that international flights from King Khalid International Airport would resume from Terminal 2 on Sunday, while Terminal 1 would be designated for domestic flights.
This follows the suspension of flights from the Riyadh airport after waves of Houthi strikes, including one on October 10 that killed 13 people and wounded hundreds.
Early Sunday, Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree warned civilians away from the Saudi capital’s airport.
“King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh is not safe because it is a military target, and we renew our warning to airlines, employees, and travelers,” Saree stated. He also announced seven operations targeting Saudi oil facilities and military bases.
Yemen has been in a state of war since Houthi forces captured the capital Sanaa in September 2014, forcing the government to flee south.
After a brief ceasefire, fighting in Yemen has intensified after government forces attacked Sanaa International Airport to prevent a Houthi delegation arriving from Tehran.
The Houthis then launched a surprise offensive in September, capturing Yemen’s western coast, including the city of Mocha.
Forces aligned with the internationally recognised government launched “Operation Dawn of Yemen” on October 5, aimed at retaking territories lost to the Houthis.
On Sunday, Yemen’s armed forces said the military had carried out 736 strikes on Houthi positions over the past 24 hours, leading to 307 people being “neutralised” and the destruction of 68 military vehicles.
Amid the military escalation, the Rasd Organization for Rights and Freedoms has warned of the dire humanitarian situation in the city of Taiz, which is under a Houthi siege.
“About 1,110 kidney failure patients face the risks of a shortage of dialysis supplies, given the need for about 120 dialysis sessions daily along with 192 patients in intensive care units and 154 children in incubators, due to the Houthi siege imposed on the city of Taiz since October 4,” the group said.

articles.title: Gaza’s visually and hearing-impaired children miss school due to Israel war
articles.source: Al Jazeera – Breaking News, World News and Video from Al Jazeera
articles.snippet: Children in Gaza with auditory and visual challenges often have no access to specialist education.
articles.full_text:
Gaza’s visually and hearing-impaired children miss school due to Israel war
Children in Gaza with auditory and visual challenges often have no access to specialist education.
Gaza City – With the help of his father, 13-year-old Kenan al-Sabaa attempts to adjust his hearing aid, which has malfunctioned. The plastic tubing and rubber ear mould on the device need fixing, but these parts and the depleted batteries are no longer available due to Israel’s siege on the Gaza Strip.
Before Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza started in October 2023, Kenan attended the Atfaluna Society for Deaf Children, which provided specialist teaching and opportunities to communicate with other hearing-impaired children.
Recommended Stories

- list 2 of 3Why is Israel launching a new military operation in the occupied West Bank?
- list 3 of 3Severe hunger stalks people in Gaza as bakeries close down
But Atfaluna’s building in Gaza City was partially levelled during the war and quickly turned into an overcrowded shelter for displaced people, an example of the widespread destruction of infrastructure in Gaza. This includes the educational institutions disabled children rely upon.
Israeli attacks also forced Kenan’s family to flee to Gaza City’s Jalaa Street. Atfaluna has since set up temporary learning spaces, and Kenan has access to one near where his family now lives. But his father, Tamer al-Sabaa, said the interruptions to his learning during the war have left his son far behind in his studies.
He did not attend school at all during the first year of the war, and now attends classes only for a few hours a week, which Tamer says is not enough given the time he has lost at school during the war.
But Tamer fears that if Israel resumes large-scale attacks – an October 2025 “ceasefire” reduced the number of attacks but did not stop them – he will be forced to stop Kenan from attending.
“These few hours do not cover or repair the massive educational gap and academic decline my son experienced during the war,” Tamer said. “He is in dire need of restoring his equipped educational environment and the specialised care that was stripped away from him.”
“The school operates only three days a week, and for limited hours not exceeding two hours a day,” he told Al Jazeera.
“Being deaf makes Kenan’s movements fraught with danger, as he cannot hear the sounds of explosions, warning signals, or communicate with those around him.”
As a result, Tamer and his wife had to guide Kenan through unfamiliar neighbourhoods to help him learn about his surroundings.
Kenan can now reach school independently, but his safety is always a concern for his parents.
Little help available
The difficulties facing Kenan highlight the effect of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, on disabled children in the enclave.
Fadel Kuraz, a sign language interpreter and disability rights advocate with Atfaluna, said the war has increased hearing-related injuries and severely weakened the services available to children who need support.
“What we are experiencing today in the Gaza Strip represents an unprecedented health and humanitarian setback, and a real catastrophe unlike anything we have seen before,” Kuraz told Al Jazeera.
“To grasp the scale of the tragedy, the baseline number of persons with hearing disabilities registered before October 2023 was around 20,000 people. Today, according to field assessments, approximately 35,000 new individuals … have been added, having suffered total or partial hearing loss due to … explosions.”
Kuraz describes shortages of hearing aids, batteries, ear moulds, and spare parts, alongside major obstacles to specialist hearing tests and treatments. Children also face difficulties accessing visual learning materials because of electricity and communications outages, he said.
“The suffering does not stop at material needs. A deaf child suffers high levels of fear, stress and complex trauma without the ability to verbally express what is on their mind,” Kuraz told Al Jazeera.
Hearing-impaired children in Gaza are more often than not living in overcrowded tents or shelters which lack privacy or a proper space to do homework and study.
“I emphasise that responding to the needs of persons with hearing disabilities is no longer a secondary choice or a luxury; it is an urgent humanitarian necessity,” Kuraz adds. “It requires immediate intervention to break the siege, allow the entry of hearing aids, batteries, and spare parts, and establish safe, temporary alternative educational spaces to replace destroyed centres.”
Generation at risk
Children with visual impairments face issues similar to those faced by hearing-impaired children in Gaza, with the few educational facilities once available to them now closed or difficult to access. The materials and items they need to study, such as Braille, are also difficult to procure due to Israel’s siege on Gaza.
Al-Noor school was originally located in Tal al-Hawa, southwest of Gaza City, but was badly damaged in the genocidal war.
Duaa Omar Basheer worked as an educational counsellor at the al-Noor school for blind students in northern Gaza before the war. She said it was the only public school in Gaza designated for middle and high school students with visual impairments, but was forced to close during the war. Some primary education is available to children through educational centres run by the United Nations agency for Palestinian refugees, UNRWA.
Previously, the school served about 80 pupils from across Gaza, many of whom arrived on dedicated buses, but damaged roads and a lack of suitable transport created further barriers.
Without regular instruction, Basheer fears students could lose their Braille and independent-learning skills, which they have taken years to learn.
“We are facing an entire generation of visually-impaired individuals at risk of illiteracy and academic loss,” Basheer said.
Broken glasses
In the Shati refugee camp in Gaza City, Jana Shreim’s mother, Wafaa Shreim, says her 12-year-old daughter, who is legally blind, relies on prescription glasses with high magnification and very strong lenses. But she could still only perceive light, shapes and nearby objects.
Her glasses broke amid the harrowing mass exodus from the Shati camp during Israel’s offensive on the neighbourhood in November 2023. The family tried to fix them with wire, but the lenses were damaged beyond use, and replacement glasses were too expensive.
Since the glasses broke – and with no possibility of replacing them due to the blockade – her vision has deteriorated to the point that she can barely see.
Now, when Jana goes to unfamiliar places, she stumbles and falls. Her mother says she is bullied by other children, and that she experiences pain in her eyes when she tries to focus.
“My daughter now has to identify people by their voices,” Wafaa told Al Jazeera. “Her sister and I now act as her ‘eyes’ at every step and everywhere she goes.”
Before the war, Jana attended the al-Noor centre, travelling there on a dedicated bus service. Her school closed when it was badly damaged in Israeli bombing, leaving Jana without any access to education.
“I am currently trying to teach her at home myself using a Braille writing machine we have, so she doesn’t lose her limited educational skills,” Jana’s mother said. She also cares for another daughter with a visual impairment, making it even more difficult to provide the specialist support they both need.
“I searched extensively and knocked on the doors of many institutions and organisations concerned with visual impairment, but the bitter truth is that … we have been left entirely alone,” she said.
“My only message and wish to all responsible parties is to look at our visually impaired children with mercy: provide them with glasses and medical supplies, and open safe educational and recreational spaces that restore their basic right to life and learning.”

Portuguese police clear Lisbon housing protest camp, arrest 25
Officers baton-charge demonstrators in overnight operation as activists demand government action on soaring rents and home shortages.
Police in Portugal have cleared a camp in central Lisbon set up to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, baton-charging demonstrators and making 25 arrests.
Dozens of officers, some with police dogs, moved in on the camp in Rossio Square shortly after 2am (02:00 GMT) on Sunday.

They had warned protesters that their tents would be dismantled if they were not removed, threatening disobedience charges for those who resisted.
Protesters had pitched more than 100 tents after Saturday’s protest march by thousands along one of Lisbon’s main avenues.
A smaller camp of about 50 tents was also dismantled in Porto’s Praca D Joao I public square, where police made six arrests.

While police reported seven minor injuries among officers and protesters in the two operations, the activist group Casa para Viver (Homes to Live) said 60 people were hurt and called for a fresh protest outside parliament on Tuesday.
“Choosing the early hours of the morning to unleash dogs and baton-charge peaceful protesters is a political decision. It shows this government would rather repress those denouncing the housing crisis than address it,” the group said.
Home affordability crises
Portugal is grappling with one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises, as prices have more than doubled since 2017 while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, with young people among the hardest hit.
Protesters say soaring rents and higher living costs are squeezing households and turning housing into a growing source of discontent.

The protesters are demanding that the government scrap a bill to make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first parliamentary reading, although the far-right Chega party abstained.
The protests in Portugal echo recent demonstrations in Spain over home shortages and surging rents.

Elena Rybakina retains Ningbo title, wins first trophy as world number one
The victory helped the Kazakh take a big step towards securing the year-end number one ranking.
Elena Rybakina blazed past unseeded Canadian Leylah Fernandez 6-2 6-2 in the Ningbo Open final to retain her title and lift her first trophy as the world number one ahead of the WTA Finals next month.
The victory on Sunday also helped the Kazakh take a big step towards securing the year-end number one ranking, further burnishing a spectacular season in which she won the Australian Open title before adding the US Open crown to reach the summit.
Top seed Rybakina made the breakthrough with her trademark power in the fifth game and then unleashed a searing crosscourt backhand winner to go 4-2 up, before the 27-year-old wrapped up the opening set in only 38 minutes.
World number 30 Fernandez made a bright start to the next set but Rybakina absorbed the pressure and raised her level to force an error and break for 2-1, with the three-time Grand Slam champion breezing to victory from there.

articles.title: US military needs ‘urgent revolutionary institutional change’ to prepare for modern war, Petraeus says
articles.snippet: Ret. Army Gen. David Petraeus praised the Pentagon’s new Autonomous Warfare Command but said the U.S. must rapidly prepare for modern autonomous war.
articles.full_text:
Unmanned systems now inflict more than 90% of Russia’s casualties on the front lines in Ukraine, yet no NATO military, including America’s, has begun the overhaul that kind of war demands, Ret. Army Gen. David Petraeus said Oct. 16, weeks after the Pentagon announced a new command for autonomous warfare.
The extent of the drone war is underestimated, with Ukraine and Russia each using roughly 10,000 drones a day, the former CIA director and onetime commander of U.S. Central Command said, speaking at an American Primary Aluminum Association event in Washington.
“This is an unmanned systems war,” Petraeus said. “Tanks aren’t survivable there anymore.”
For Ukraine, drones and unmanned weapons have become central to how the country has leveraged a smaller, outgunned force against a much larger, better-financed adversary for almost five years.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy ordered the creation of a new Unmanned Systems Forces military branch in 2024, and the Defense Ministry has said time and again that developing more autonomous weapons is a top priority.
But for the rest of the world, Petraeus said, the fighting in Ukraine is a window into the future and a warning about the dangers of being underprepared for the battles to come.
“Really, no NATO country and not even the United States is undertaking yet the urgent revolutionary institutional change that should be taken based on what we see in Ukraine, which is the future of war,” he said.
The U.S. needs a new concept of warfare that runs through force structure, training, procurement, personnel policy and bases, the general said, replacing much of the legacy, heavily manned equipment with unmanned systems that are cheaper and far more numerous.
“What’s going to happen is we’ll see the introduction of autonomous systems really for the first time in warfare,” Petraeus said.
Washington is making “some commendable steps” toward developing these weapons, according to Petraeus, including establishing a new Autonomous Warfare Command that requires each military branch to stand up its own component command.
“But my hope is that they will not just create an unmanned systems force in terms of force structure, but that they will also spur the initiation of true institutional change,” Petraeus said.
That includes how the U.S. buys weapons, Petraeus said, calling for “very, very substantial manufacturing capacity but not necessarily producing all the time.”
“You want it to be able to make software changes every week, hardware changes every few weeks, which is what’s going on in Ukraine because the enemy continues to evolve and Russia’s been innovating very substantially as well,” he said.
Ukraine will produce as many as 20 million unmanned systems this year, Zelenskyy said in a July speech, with a shortage of trained operators and the acquisition of some weapons components — including optics, gimbals, brushless motors and fiber-optic cable — becoming the domestic industry’s production bottleneck.
The general also rejected the idea that the U.S. war with Iran has hurt Washington’s ability to help Kyiv, though he acknowledged the U.S. has used “a fair number of missile interceptors,” which “makes it more difficult to share those with others around the world.”
The war has consumed between one-half and two-thirds of the U.S. inventory of certain missile-defense interceptors, according to a Congressional Budget Office estimate released in September.
“We can help the Ukrainians in any way in which we decide to assist them,” Petraeus said. “These are policy decisions.”

articles.title: ‘The West can’t stop me’: Space wars heat up as Russia tails a Ukraine-linked US satellite
articles.snippet: Washington blamed Moscow for deliberately moving a Russian military satellite with an undisclosed mission close last week to a U.S.-registered satellite.
articles.full_text:
KYIV, Ukraine — Washington blamed Moscow at the United Nations on Wednesday for deliberately moving a Russian military satellite with an undisclosed mission “dangerously” close last week to a U.S.-registered satellite believed to serve Ukraine, with officials vowing to defend American interests in space.
The Russian satellite, Cosmos 2612, spent more than two weeks maneuvering toward ICEYE-X36, a radar satellite operated by the American arm of Finnish company ICEYE that supplies imagery to Ukraine’s military through some of its spacecraft, then shadowed it from as close as a third of a mile through the weekend of Oct. 17.
U.S. Undersecretary of State Thomas G. DiNanno called the Russian satellite’s behavior “threatening,” and said the country had been “intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite, behaviors consistent with on-orbit weapons operations.”
Space historian and former NASA astrophysicist Jonathan McDowell said that he believed it is the first rendezvous in low Earth orbit between two active satellites without one owner’s approval.
The close encounter came weeks after Air Force Secretary Troy Meink publicly confirmed that the U.S. has weapons in orbit and the Space Force picked two companies to build space-to-space reconnaissance satellites. It also followed reports that trillionaire Elon Musk — under White House orders — slowed the military-grade Starlink that Ukraine relies on, rendering some of the country’s essential air defense weapons useless.
The operation fits a wider Russian campaign of intimidation against Europe and the U.S. that lets Russian President Vladimir Putin “poke the West in the eye and watch the West do nothing,” according to Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“They prove a point – the West can’t stop me,” Swope added Wednesday during a CSIS panel on the encounter.
As the U.S. and its allies increasingly rely on commercial capabilities for national security, key assets like satellites have “become vulnerabilities that can be exploited by our adversary,” according to Greg Gillinger, senior vice president of strategy and development at Virginia-based Integrity ISR, who also spoke on the CSIS panel.
The impact of a possible satellite attack could reach well beyond one company or country, since commercial satellites now carry much of the imagery and connectivity militaries fight with, experts said. Musk’s Starlink slowdown in Ukraine showed how quickly a military force can suffer when that access is throttled without notice — and how easily local geopolitical conflicts can explode into global security crises.
On Oct. 12, commercial trackers feeding the U.S. military’s Joint Commercial Operations cell flagged the possible rendezvous when Cosmos 2612 slid into ICEYE-X36’s orbit roughly 345 miles above Earth, according to Integrity ISR’s newsletter.
On Oct. 15 and 16, the Russian satellite moved from more than 200 miles behind ICEYE-X36 to roughly 3 miles away before moving in closer and holding position through the weekend, tracking firm LeoLabs said in a statement reported by CNN.
Both satellites travel at roughly 4 miles (7 kilometers) per second, so getting two objects “within a hundred meters or even a kilometer” of each other is “the equivalent of flying in a very tight formation in an aircraft,” Gillinger said.
“Russia didn’t accidentally get within a kilometer of X36,” he said. “It is an indication of intent that they’re sending a message.”
ICEYE, whose radar satellites see through clouds, smoke and darkness, expanded cooperation with Ukraine’s military, pledging continued imagery “on tactical timelines,” according to a January statement. However, the company has not confirmed which of its satellites serve Kyiv.
Moscow has warned since the first year of its full-scale invasion that Western commercial satellites helping Ukraine could become legitimate military targets.
ICEYE said it is “aware of the situation and tracking it closely” and that its “constellation architecture is designed for continuity and resilience,” a spokesperson told Air & Space Forces Magazine earlier this week.
Russia’s intent behind the satellite maneuvers remains unclear. According to LeoLabs, an American space technology company, possible aims range from intelligence collection and close inspection to coercion and groundwork for future operations against satellites.
The maneuvers demonstrated capabilities that could be used to “inspect, characterize, shadow, or potentially interfere with another spacecraft,” though they “do not establish hostile intent,” the company said.
Analysts could not yet say whether Moscow planned an attack and then reversed course, or was orbiting nearby for another purpose entirely.
Russia could have been doing “a dry run” for a future attack, or the satellite could have been carrying a weapon, from a jammer to a laser to a projectile, Swope explained.
“Was the intent to blow up the satellite? No,” he said. “Was the intent to put some type of energy on the satellite? Probably… I don’t know why you’d need to maneuver in this way, this close, unless you wanted to do something that involved putting energy on that satellite.”
The Russian satellite has since pulled back, but not far.
It was again flying at ICEYE-X36’s altitude on Wednesday, holding roughly 250 miles (400 kilometers) behind it, and could “easily close that gap again at the time and place of their choosing,” Gillinger said.
Russia could try to approach another ICEYE satellite within weeks, as two more satellites from the same launch will soon line up with the orbit of a second satellite, ICEYE-X37, according to Integrity ISR.
If they move in, “we could see another scenario where another commercial satellite is closely trailed by one of these Russian satellites,” Gillinger said.
The retreat began Oct. 18, two days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order waiving tariffs and most economic restrictions on Russia.
Swope said Trump’s move to ease sanctions “could have been a reason why Putin said, ‘You know, now’s not the time to exacerbate tensions specifically with the United States. Maybe we should pause this operation.’”
“If you’re getting close to a deal on something, why jeopardize that?” he said.
The potential for a conflict in space has been growing in recent months.
Washington “appears to lack response options” if Russia threatened U.S. military and commercial satellites with a nuclear weapon in orbit, according to the conclusions from a 2025 war-game scenario where fictional Russian space objects threatened American interests.
There is no public indication that Cosmos 2612 carries a nuclear weapon, but Swope said that there is also still no internationally recognized rule for determining if a maneuver like this one should be considered hostile — or what international standards should be followed in a response.
“Even though we all can make a good case on why this was [hostile], there’s no norm that you could point to,” he said.
Without a clear response plan or real consequences for aggression, menacing satellite moves like this one are “literally just a spigot that Russia could turn on and off” to increase pressure on adversaries, Swope said.
Russia, he added, “is going to turn it on again.”
