Space
Space is a three-dimensional continuum containing positions and directions.[1] In classical physics, physical space is often conceived in three linear dimensions. Modern physicists usually consider it, with time, to be part of a boundless four-dimensional continuum known as spacetime.[2] The concept of space is considered to be of fundamental importance to an understanding of the physical universe. However, disagreement continues between philosophers over whether it is itself an entity, a relationship between entities, or part of a conceptual framework.
In the 19th and 20th centuries mathematicians began to examine geometries that are non-Euclidean, in which space is conceived as curved, rather than flat, as in the Euclidean space. According to Albert Einstein's theory of general relativity, space around gravitational fields deviates from Euclidean space.[3] Experimental tests of general relativity have confirmed that non-Euclidean geometries provide a better model for the shape of space.[citation needed]
Philosophy of space
Debates concerning the nature, essence and the mode of existence of space date back to antiquity; namely, to treatises like the Timaeus of Plato, or Socrates in his reflections on what the Greeks called khôra (i.e. "space"), or in the Physics of Aristotle (Book IV, Delta) in the definition of topos (i.e. place), or in the later "geometrical conception of place" as "space qua extension" in the Discourse on Place (Qawl fi al-Makan) of the 11th-century Arab polymath Alhazen.[4] Many of these classical philosophical questions were discussed in the Renaissance and then reformulated in the 17th century, particularly during the early development of classical mechanics.
Isaac Newton viewed space as absolute, existing permanently and independently of whether there was any matter in it.[5] In contrast, other natural philosophers, notably Gottfried Leibniz, thought that space was in fact a collection of relations between objects, given by their distance and direction from one another. In the 18th century, the philosopher and theologian George Berkeley attempted to refute the "visibility of spatial depth" in his Essay Towards a New Theory of Vision. Later, the metaphysician Immanuel Kant said that the concepts of space and time are not empirical ones derived from experiences of the outside world—they are elements of an already given systematic framework that humans possess and use to structure all experiences. Kant referred to the experience of "space" in his Critique of Pure Reason as being a subjective "pure a priori form of intuition".
Galileo
Galilean and Cartesian theories about space, matter, and motion are at the foundation of the Scientific Revolution, which is understood to have culminated with the publication of Newton's Principia Mathematica in 1687.[6] Newton's theories about space and time helped him explain the movement of objects. While his theory of space is considered the most influential in physics, it emerged from his predecessors' ideas about the same.[7]
As one of the pioneers of modern science, Galileo revised the established Aristotelian and Ptolemaic ideas about a geocentric cosmos. He backed the Copernican theory that the universe was heliocentric, with a stationary Sun at the center and the planets—including the Earth—revolving around the Sun. If the Earth moved, the Aristotelian belief that its natural tendency was to remain at rest was in question. Galileo wanted to prove instead that the Sun moved around its axis, that motion was as natural to an object as the state of rest. In other words, for Galileo, celestial bodies, including the Earth, were naturally inclined to move in circles. This view displaced another Aristotelian idea—that all objects gravitated towards their designated natural place-of-belonging.[8]
René Descartes
Descartes set out to replace the Aristotelian worldview with a theory about space and motion as determined by natural laws. In other words, he sought a metaphysical foundation or a mechanical explanation for his theories about matter and motion. Cartesian space was Euclidean in structure—infinite, uniform and flat.[9] It was defined as that which contained matter; conversely, matter by definition had a spatial extension so that there was no such thing as empty space.[6]
The Cartesian notion of space is closely linked to his theories about the nature of the body, mind and matter. He is famously known for his "cogito ergo sum" (I think therefore I am), or the idea that we can only be certain of the fact that we can doubt, and therefore think and therefore exist. His theories belong to the rationalist tradition, which attributes knowledge about the world to our ability to think rather than to our experiences, as the empiricists believe.[10] He posited a clear distinction between the body and mind, which is referred to as the Cartesian dualism.
Leibniz and Newton
Following Galileo and Descartes, during the seventeenth century the philosophy of space and time revolved around the ideas of Gottfried Leibniz, a German philosopher–mathematician, and Isaac Newton, who set out two opposing theories of what space is. Rather than being an entity that independently exists over and above other matter, Leibniz held that space is no more than the collection of spatial relations between objects in the world: "space is that which results from places taken together".[11] Unoccupied regions are those that could have objects in them, and thus spatial relations with other places. For Leibniz, then, space was an idealised abstraction from the relations between individual entities or their possible locations and therefore could not be continuous but must be discrete.[12] Space could be thought of in a similar way to the relations between family members. Although people in the family are related to one another, the relations do not exist independently of the people.[13] Leibniz argued that space could not exist independently of objects in the world because that implies a difference between two universes exactly alike except for the location of the material world in each universe. But since there would be no observational way of telling these universes apart then, according to the identity of indiscernibles, there would be no real difference between them. According to the principle of sufficient reason, any theory of space that implied that there could be these two possible universes must therefore be wrong.[14]
Newton took space to be more than relations between material objects and based his position on observation and experimentation. For a relationist there can be no real difference between inertial motion, in which the object travels with constant velocity, and non-inertial motion, in which the velocity changes with time, since all spatial measurements are relative to other objects and their motions. But Newton argued that since non-inertial motion generates forces, it must be absolute.[15] He used the example of water in a spinning bucket to demonstrate his argument. Water in a bucket is hung from a rope and set to spin, starts with a flat surface. After a while, as the bucket continues to spin, the surface of the water becomes concave. If the bucket's spinning is stopped then the surface of the water remains concave as it continues to spin. The concave surface is therefore apparently not the result of relative motion between the bucket and the water.[16] Instead, Newton argued, it must be a result of non-inertial motion relative to space itself. For several centuries the bucket argument was considered decisive in showing that space must exist independently of matter.
Kant
In the eighteenth century the German philosopher Immanuel Kant published his theory of space as "a property of our mind" by which "we represent to ourselves objects as outside us, and all as in space" in the Critique of Pure Reason[17] On his view the nature of spatial predicates are "relations that only attach to the form of intuition alone, and thus to the subjective constitution of our mind, without which these predicates could not be attached to anything at all."[18] This develops his theory of knowledge in which knowledge about space itself can be both a priori and synthetic.[19] According to Kant, knowledge about space is synthetic because any proposition about space cannot be true merely in virtue of the meaning of the terms contained in the proposition. In the counter-example, the proposition "all unmarried men are bachelors" is true by virtue of each term's meaning. Further, space is a priori because it is the form of our receptive abilities to receive information about the external world. For example, someone without sight can still perceive spatial attributes via touch, hearing, and smell. Knowledge of space itself is a priori because it belongs to the subjective constitution of our mind as the form or manner of our intuition of external objects.
Non-Euclidean geometry
Euclid's Elements contained five postulates that form the basis for Euclidean geometry. One of these, the parallel postulate, has been the subject of debate among mathematicians for many centuries. It states that on any plane on which there is a straight line L1 and a point P not on L1, there is exactly one straight line L2 on the plane that passes through the point P and is parallel to the straight line L1. Until the 19th century, few doubted the truth of the postulate; instead debate centered over whether it was necessary as an axiom, or whether it was a theory that could be derived from the other axioms.[20] Around 1830 though, the Hungarian János Bolyai and the Russian Nikolai Ivanovich Lobachevsky separately published treatises on a type of geometry that does not include the parallel postulate, called hyperbolic geometry. In this geometry, an infinite number of parallel lines pass through the point P. Consequently, the sum of angles in a triangle is less than 180° and the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter is greater than pi. In the 1850s, Bernhard Riemann developed an equivalent theory of elliptical geometry, in which no parallel lines pass through P. In this geometry, triangles have more than 180° and circles have a ratio of circumference-to-diameter that is less than pi.
Type of geometry | Number of parallels | Sum of angles in a triangle | Ratio of circumference to diameter of circle | Measure of curvature |
---|---|---|---|---|
Hyperbolic | Infinite | < 180° | > π | < 0 |
Euclidean | 1 | 180° | π | 0 |
Elliptical | 0 | > 180° | < π | > 0 |
Gauss and Poincaré
Although there was a prevailing Kantian consensus at the time, once non-Euclidean geometries had been formalised, some began to wonder whether or not physical space is curved. Carl Friedrich Gauss, a German mathematician, was the first to consider an empirical investigation of the geometrical structure of space. He thought of making a test of the sum of the angles of an enormous stellar triangle, and there are reports that he actually carried out a test, on a small scale, by triangulating mountain tops in Germany.[21]
Henri Poincaré, a French mathematician and physicist of the late 19th century, introduced an important insight in which he attempted to demonstrate the futility of any attempt to discover which geometry applies to space by experiment.[22] He considered the predicament that would face scientists if they were confined to the surface of an imaginary large sphere with particular properties, known as a sphere-world. In this world, the temperature is taken to vary in such a way that all objects expand and contract in similar proportions in different places on the sphere. With a suitable falloff in temperature, if the scientists try to use measuring rods to determine the sum of the angles in a triangle, they can be deceived into thinking that they inhabit a plane, rather than a spherical surface.[23] In fact, the scientists cannot in principle determine whether they inhabit a plane or sphere and, Poincaré argued, the same is true for the debate over whether real space is Euclidean or not. For him, which geometry was used to describe space was a matter of convention.[24] Since Euclidean geometry is simpler than non-Euclidean geometry, he assumed the former would always be used to describe the 'true' geometry of the world.[25]
Einstein
In 1905, Albert Einstein published his special theory of relativity, which led to the concept that space and time can be viewed as a single construct known as spacetime. In this theory, the speed of light in vacuum is the same for all observers—which has the result that two events that appear simultaneous to one particular observer will not be simultaneous to another observer if the observers are moving with respect to one another. Moreover, an observer will measure a moving clock to tick more slowly than one that is stationary with respect to them; and objects are measured to be shortened in the direction that they are moving with respect to the observer.
Subsequently, Einstein worked on a general theory of relativity, which is a theory of how gravity interacts with spacetime. Instead of viewing gravity as a force field acting in spacetime, Einstein suggested that it modifies the geometric structure of spacetime itself.[26] According to the general theory, time goes more slowly at places with lower gravitational potentials and rays of light bend in the presence of a gravitational field. Scientists have studied the behaviour of binary pulsars, confirming the predictions of Einstein's theories.[27] Non-Euclidean geometry is usually used to describe spacetime.[28]
Mathematics
In modern mathematics spaces are defined as sets with some added structure. They are typically topological spaces, in which a concept of neighbourhood is defined, frequently by means of a distance (metric spaces). The elements of a space are often called points, but they can have other names such as vectors in vector spaces and functions in function spaces.
Physics
This section needs more citations. (April 2020) |
Part of a series on |
Classical mechanics |
---|
Space is one of the few fundamental quantities in physics, meaning that it cannot be defined via other quantities because nothing more fundamental is known at the present. On the other hand, it can be related to other fundamental quantities. Thus, similar to other fundamental quantities (like time and mass), space can be explored via measurement and experiment.[29]
Today, our three-dimensional space is viewed as embedded in a four-dimensional spacetime, called Minkowski space (see special relativity). The idea behind spacetime is that time is hyperbolic-orthogonal to each of the three spatial dimensions.
Relativity
This section needs more citations. (April 2020) |
Before Albert Einstein's work on relativistic physics, time and space were viewed as independent dimensions. Einstein's discoveries showed that due to relativity of motion our space and time can be mathematically combined into one object–spacetime. It turns out that distances in space or in time separately are not invariant with respect to Lorentz coordinate transformations, but distances in Minkowski space along spacetime intervals are—which justifies the name.[citation needed]
In addition, time and space dimensions should not be viewed as exactly equivalent in Minkowski space. One can freely move in space but not in time. Thus, time and space coordinates are treated differently both in special relativity (where time is sometimes considered an imaginary coordinate) and in general relativity (where different signs are assigned to time and space components of spacetime metric).[citation needed]
Furthermore, in Einstein's general theory of relativity, it is postulated that spacetime is geometrically distorted – curved – near to gravitationally significant masses.[30]
One consequence of this postulate, which follows from the equations of general relativity, is the prediction of moving ripples of spacetime, called gravitational waves. While indirect evidence for these waves has been found (in the motions of the Hulse–Taylor binary system, for example) experiments attempting to directly measure these waves are ongoing at the LIGO and Virgo collaborations. LIGO scientists reported the first such direct observation of gravitational waves on 14 September 2015.[31][32]
Cosmology
This section needs more citations. (April 2020) |
Relativity theory leads to the cosmological question of what shape the universe is, and where space came from. It appears that space was created in the Big Bang, 13.8 billion years ago[33] and has been expanding ever since. The overall shape of space is not known, but space is known to be expanding very rapidly due to the cosmic inflation.
Spatial measurement
This section needs more citations. (April 2020) |
The measurement of physical space has long been important. Although earlier societies had developed measuring systems, the International System of Units, (SI), is now the most common system of units used in the measuring of space, and is almost universally used.
Currently, the standard space interval, called a standard meter or simply meter, is defined as the distance traveled by light in vacuum during a time interval of exactly 1/299,792,458 of a second. This definition coupled with present definition of the second is based on the special theory of relativity in which the speed of light plays the role of a fundamental constant of nature.
Geographical space
This section needs more citations. (April 2020) |
Geography is the branch of science concerned with identifying and describing places on Earth, utilizing spatial awareness to try to understand why things exist in specific locations. Cartography is the mapping of spaces to allow better navigation, for visualization purposes and to act as a locational device. Geostatistics apply statistical concepts to collected spatial data of Earth to create an estimate for unobserved phenomena.
Geographical space is often considered as land, and can have a relation to ownership usage (in which space is seen as property or territory). While some cultures assert the rights of the individual in terms of ownership, other cultures will identify with a communal approach to land ownership, while still other cultures such as Australian Aboriginals, rather than asserting ownership rights to land, invert the relationship and consider that they are in fact owned by the land. Spatial planning is a method of regulating the use of space at land-level, with decisions made at regional, national and international levels. Space can also impact on human and cultural behavior, being an important factor in architecture, where it will impact on the design of buildings and structures, and on farming.
Ownership of space is not restricted to land. Ownership of airspace and of waters is decided internationally. Other forms of ownership have been recently asserted to other spaces—for example to the radio bands of the electromagnetic spectrum or to cyberspace.
Public space is a term used to define areas of land as collectively owned by the community, and managed in their name by delegated bodies; such spaces are open to all, while private property is the land culturally owned by an individual or company, for their own use and pleasure.
Abstract space is a term used in geography to refer to a hypothetical space characterized by complete homogeneity. When modeling activity or behavior, it is a conceptual tool used to limit extraneous variables such as terrain.
In psychology
This section needs more citations. (April 2020) |
Psychologists first began to study the way space is perceived in the middle of the 19th century. Those now concerned with such studies regard it as a distinct branch of psychology. Psychologists analyzing the perception of space are concerned with how recognition of an object's physical appearance or its interactions are perceived, see, for example, visual space.
Other, more specialized topics studied include amodal perception and object permanence. The perception of surroundings is important due to its necessary relevance to survival, especially with regards to hunting and self preservation as well as simply one's idea of personal space.
Several space-related phobias have been identified, including agoraphobia (the fear of open spaces), astrophobia (the fear of celestial space) and claustrophobia (the fear of enclosed spaces).
The understanding of three-dimensional space in humans is thought to be learned during infancy using unconscious inference, and is closely related to hand-eye coordination. The visual ability to perceive the world in three dimensions is called depth perception.
In the social sciences
Space has been studied in the social sciences from the perspectives of Marxism, feminism, postmodernism, postcolonialism, urban theory and critical geography. These theories account for the effect of the history of colonialism, transatlantic slavery and globalization on our understanding and experience of space and place. The topic has garnered attention since the 1980s, after the publication of Henri Lefebvre's The Production of Space . In this book, Lefebvre applies Marxist ideas about the production of commodities and accumulation of capital to discuss space as a social product. His focus is on the multiple and overlapping social processes that produce space.[34]
In his book The Condition of Postmodernity, David Harvey describes what he terms the "time-space compression." This is the effect of technological advances and capitalism on our perception of time, space and distance.[35] Changes in the modes of production and consumption of capital affect and are affected by developments in transportation and technology. These advances create relationships across time and space, new markets and groups of wealthy elites in urban centers, all of which annihilate distances and affect our perception of linearity and distance.[36]
In his book Thirdspace, Edward Soja describes space and spatiality as an integral and neglected aspect of what he calls the "trialectics of being," the three modes that determine how we inhabit, experience and understand the world. He argues that critical theories in the Humanities and Social Sciences study the historical and social dimensions of our lived experience, neglecting the spatial dimension.[37] He builds on Henri Lefebvre's work to address the dualistic way in which humans understand space—as either material/physical or as represented/imagined. Lefebvre's "lived space"[38] and Soja's "thirdspace" are terms that account for the complex ways in which humans understand and navigate place, which "firstspace" and "Secondspace" (Soja's terms for material and imagined spaces respectively) do not fully encompass.
Postcolonial theorist Homi Bhabha's concept of Third Space is different from Soja's Thirdspace, even though both terms offer a way to think outside the terms of a binary logic. Bhabha's Third Space is the space in which hybrid cultural forms and identities exist. In his theories, the term hybrid describes new cultural forms that emerge through the interaction between colonizer and colonized.[39]

articles.full_text:
PARIS — France and the United Kingdom carried out a joint airborne nuclear strike exercise for the first time, with Eurofighter Typhoon jets from the Royal Air Force escorting French Rafale jets on a simulated nuclear-strike mission.
The French and British fighter jets flew a joint mission on Tuesday during the exercise Rummy, the French Armed Forces Ministry said in a statement on Friday, calling the drill a show of growing cooperation in the framework of an agreement last year for closer nuclear cooperation and coordination between the two countries.
France is working with several European allies on a concept of “forward deterrence” amid uncertainty around United States security guarantees for Europe in the face of an aggressive Russia. While both France and the U.K. operate strategic ballistic-missile submarines as a nuclear deterrent, France has an airborne component, which the U.K. lacks, in the shape of Rafale jets carrying nuclear-tipped cruise missiles.
“Having independent nuclear forces doesn’t exclude coordination,” French Armed Forces Minister Catherine Vautrin said. “By coordinating, our nuclear forces demonstrate that they can contribute even more significantly to the overall security of the alliance and the peace and stability of the Euro-Atlantic zone.”
The British aircraft operated alongside those of France’s Strategic Air Forces over the Mediterranean, with Typhoons escorting Rafale fighters, according to the ministry. While the Rafale jets performed a simulated nuclear strike, the exercise didn’t involve any actual nuclear weapons, the ministry said.
In addition to Eurofighter Typhoon and Rafale jets, the exercise included A330 MRTT tanker aircraft, French Armed Forces Chief of Staff Gen. Fabien Mandon said in a post on the social network X. The French and British crews took off from Saint-Dizier air base in northeastern France, and showed a “very high level of interoperability and a capability to coordinate,” he said.
Mandon’s post included a picture showing three taxiing Eurofighters, as well as a Eurofighter under a hard cover with the markings of the RAF 29 Squadron.
“This is a revolution for the Strategic Air Forces, which have always operated in complete autonomy since their creation in the 1960s,” said Etienne Marcuz, a senior analyst at the Fondation pour la Recherche Stratégique, in a post on X. He called the involvement of at least three British Eurofighter aircraft “quite significant.”
The exercise was an important step in the implementation of the Northwood Declaration, showing a determination to deter common threats together, the ministry said. France and the U.K. last year agreed to deepen nuclear cooperation and coordination, stating in the declaration that they agreed there was no extreme threat to Europe that would not prompt a response by both nations.
The exercise Rummy took place on Oct. 20 and 21, according to the ministry. France’s Air and Space Force regularly holds simulated nuclear-strike exercises called Poker.
The U.K. and France maintain sovereign and independent nuclear forces, and decision-making regarding their use isn’t shared, the ministry said. The countries would only consider using nuclear weapons in “extreme circumstances of legitimate defense,” the French ministry said.

articles.title: US Air Force wants AI to assist aerial refueling
articles.snippet: The goal is for AI to automatically analyze refueling operations from cameras mounted on the tankers and provide “hot wash” feedback to the tanker crews.
articles.full_text:
The U.S. Air Force is looking to artificial intelligence to improve the performance of its aerial refueling crews.
The goal is for AI to automatically analyze refueling operations from cameras mounted on the tankers and provide “hot wash” feedback to the tanker crews.
According to an Air Force Small Business Innovation Research solicitation, the service wants a system that can “leverage advanced computer vision, machine learning, and aviation (flight dynamics) analytics techniques to automatically extract operationally relevant performance metrics from aerial refueling events, quantify deviations from desired flight profiles, and generate actionable post-flight feedback to improve aircrew proficiency, reduce human-factor-driven mishaps, and enhance mission readiness.”
The application deadline is Nov. 25.
The SBIR is focused on the KC-46 tanker, which will feature a remote vision system that will allow operators to remotely operate the refueling boom via cameras and a 3D display. Though the system has been plagued by teething problems, the Air Force says most will soon be resolved.
The system would automatically track the tanker and refueling boom, as well as the receiving aircraft. It would measure a variety of data, including position, velocity, alignment and closure rate, and assess whether they deviate from nominal parameters.
The Air Force hopes an AI-based assessment system will mitigate the biases inherent in human assessment of aerial refueling, which is among the most demanding tasks for aircrew.
“Current aerial refueling training and post-flight assessment processes rely heavily on instructor observation, pilot self-assessment, manual video review, and subjective evaluation of performance,” the SBIR noted.
The system would create visual displays to improve the performance of pilots of the aircraft receiving fuel, such as “graphic AI overlays, heat maps, event timelines, and immersive or interactive debrief environments.” It would also have the potential to integrate with other training systems, including virtual and augmented reality, simulators, mission rehearsal systems, and other computer-based training tools.
The Air Force sees this as a prototype for future AI-based training systems.
“The desired end state is an operationally demonstrated capability ready to implement for at least one type of receiver aircraft and that can support transition into existing aviation training ecosystems and provide a scalable foundation for future AI-enabled aviation performance assessment across the Department of Defense,” the solicitation reads.

articles.title: Saudi missile plant expansion may produce more powerful missiles, study says
articles.snippet: More capable missiles could help Saudi Arabia deter Iranian attacks and make its military more self-reliant, but they risk fueling a regional missile race.
articles.full_text:
Saudi Arabia appears to be expanding its ballistic missile factory to build larger solid-fuel missiles that could fly farther or carry heavier payloads, according to two U.S. researchers who analyzed more than a year of commercial satellite images.
More capable missiles could help Saudi Arabia to deter attacks by Iran and make its military more self-reliant, while possibly strengthening its position in a deadly conflict with Yemen’s Tehran-backed Houthi fighters.
But they risk fueling a regional missile race and could deepen opposition in the U.S. Congress to a U.S.-Saudi civilian nuclear agreement that has already raised concerns about proliferation.
Satellite company Planet Labs, based in the U.S., took images of the al-Duwadimi complex about 125 miles west of Riyadh between April 2025 and September 2026.
The two researchers, Sam Lair and Michael Duitsman of the Foreign Policy Research Institute, assessed that those images show a new building that houses casting pits — wells in which a mixture of fuel ingredients is poured into missile motor casings and allowed to harden.
The Saudi embassy and Information Ministry did not respond to requests for comment.
The building, flanked by what appear to be walls to protect nearby structures from accidental explosions, is at least twice as large as the one believed to house the plant’s existing casting pits, Lair and Duitsman said in their assessment. The Foreign Policy Research Institute (FPRI) is a non-partisan research organization in Philadelphia.
A second new building could be used to store fuel ingredients or finished missile components, they said.
The imagery “suggests that Saudi Arabia is expanding the infrastructure at the missile production complex, likely to produce larger missiles which could deliver larger payloads or reach longer ranges,” they wrote.
Militaries favor solid-fuel missiles because they can be stored for long periods and launched more quickly than liquid-fuel systems.
Lair and Duitsman and experts from the London-based International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) and the CNA research and analysis organization told Reuters that the makeup of Saudi Arabia’s missile force suggests that the al-Duwadimi complex relies on Chinese technology. Lair and Duitsman said that its characteristics are also similar to Chinese missile plants.
Saudi Arabia secretly acquired about 40 liquid-fuel DF-3 ballistic missiles from China in 1987, according to a 1991 declassified CIA estimate. It displayed two of them for the first time in an April 2014 military parade, according to a YouTube video and photographs of the event.
The FPRI team also recently identified from social media videos and photos what they assessed was the wreckage in Yemen of a Saudi-fired Chinese-designed DF-15 missile.
Lair said the kingdom may now be producing the solid-fuel DF-15, and that the expansion of a1-Dumadimi is likely for the production of the longer-range DF-21 or a similar missile.
Riyadh is believed to have turned to Beijing because Washington has long restricted exports of longer-range missile systems.
The Chinese embassy and defense ministry did not respond to requests for comment. The CIA declined to comment. The White House did not respond to a request for comment.
Missiles would alter the balance of power
Sascha Bruchmann, a research fellow at IISS, said longer-range missiles would allow Saudi Arabia to strike Iran without risking its U.S.-supplied F-15 jet fighters against Iranian air defenses.
“You’d want a system to threaten whatever is holy to Tehran … if you don’t have the political will to send an F-15 with JDAMs over Tehran,” said Bruchmann, referring to U.S.-made satellite-guided bombs. “Iran has a lead because its missiles and drones can strike Saudi wherever it wants. The Saudis could close that capability gap a bit.”
Bruchmann, who reviewed the FPRI analysis at Reuters request, concurred that the expansion of al-Duwadimi could be for producing more powerful solid-fuel missiles.
Janes, the defense intelligence company, also reviewed it and said the buildings “may suggest an effort to expand production capability or support the development of longer-range missiles.”
Saudi Arabia’s apparent pursuit of more powerful missiles comes as other Gulf powers are also seeking to expand their offensive and defensive arsenals, said Decker Eveleth, a CNA analyst who has been tracking the al-Duwadimi construction with commercial satellite imagery and concurred with the FPRI assessment.
“This is being replicated across the Middle East,” he said. “You see exactly the same thing happening in the UAE. You see the exact same thing happening in Turkey. Everybody is doing this now.”
The expansion of al-Duwadimi could have political consequences in the US by stiffening bipartisan congressional opposition to a US-Saudi agreement under which the US would help Riyadh establish uranium enrichment for power generation.
Opponents say that the deal lacks sufficient safeguards to prevent Riyadh from secretly building a nuclear weapon. The kingdom has denied any such plan.
Work began last year
The FPRI assessment said the Planet Labs imagery showed that the expansion at al-Duwadimi began in April 2025 with ground-clearing and digging for the suspected storage building. Work on the suspected casting-pit building began later that month or in early May, it said.
A December 12, 2025, photo showed what researchers assessed were two deep pits inside the building that had no roof yet.
A Sept. 18, 2026, photo shows the roof still partly missing and “heavy duty blast diverting walls” on either side to prevent accidental explosions from damaging adjacent structures.
The walls, the researchers said, are somewhat similar to those depicted in imagery of US and Iranian missile plants and “further evidence the building is for casting solid propellant motors.”
Finishing the roofs would not take long, the FPRI said, but installing casting equipment may take several months. The facility could be ready to start producing missiles as early as the end of the year.

articles.title: China’s first aircraft carrier forms ‘evolving pattern’ of voyages in disputed Asian seas
articles.snippet: The carrier group’s passages not far from Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines have raised alerts.
articles.full_text:
NEW TAIPEI CITY, Taiwan— China’s first aircraft carrier, heavily watched around East Asia as an emblem of Beijing’s growing naval power, had made at least six faraway deployments since its completion 14 years ago.
It made another in October.
So frequent are the Chinese aircraft carrier CNS Liaoning’s publicly visible voyages that military analysts presume that the People’s Liberation Army Navy has fixed a routine that will let the relatively aged carrier help train and equip the fleet’s two more modern ones.
Still, the carrier group’s passages not far from Taiwan, Japan and the Philippines – places that have political or maritime sovereignty disputes with China – have raised alerts.
“The current voyage by the Liaoning appears to be part of an established evolving pattern of far-seas training deployments,” said Carl Thayer, an Asia specialist and emeritus professor at the University of New South Wales in Australia.
“The Liaoning demonstrates China’s naval military capability and political influence through its constant presence in China’s near and far seas,” he said.
The aircraft carrier led a naval task group to the western Pacific Ocean on Oct. 14 for training, the Chinese People’s Liberation Army Navy said via China’s official Xinhua News Agency. Citing the navy, Xinhua called the expedition a “drill” and part of an annual routine training plan aimed at “testing and improving combat readiness.”
China’s state-controlled Global Times news outlet called the Liaoning’s October voyage its second in the distant seas and hailed the carrier’s long-term progress as going from a “coastal pathfinder” to a “far-sea blade.”
The vessel, categorized as a “short take-off but arrested recovery” aircraft carrier, measures about 305 meters (1,000 feet) long and with flight deck width up to 75 meters.
As of Oct. 23, the carrier group had done exercises near the southernmost Japanese outlying islands and was headed for the South China Sea near the Philippines, according to local media reports in East Asia. The reports said it went with two large destroyers and a guided-missile destroyer.
The deployments are meant to show China’s two more-modern carriers, the CNS Fujian and the CNS Shandong, how to adopt new technology, experts said.
The nine-year-old Shandong carrier would learn about “new and emerging” technology as the older Liaoning tests flight operations, sensors and modern aircraft, said Collin Koh, a senior fellow at Nanyang Technological University in Singapore.
“The Shandong aircraft carrier is basically an improved version of the Liaoning,” Koh said. He said the current deployment was probably “meant maybe to validate certain technologies.”
Being the oldest of China’s three carriers, the Liaoning would “not be the frontline reaction force if there were a contingency”, said Alexander Huang, chairman of the Council of Strategic and Wargaming Studies in Taipei.
China’s maritime rivals have taken notice.
The Taiwan Ministry of National Defense said in mid-October it was monitoring the possibility of large-scale Chinese military exercises nearby as an outcome of the Liaoning’s movements.
China claims self-ruled Taiwan as part of its territory and has not ruled out the use of force to take it. The PLA has stepped up military activity in waters near the island since 2022.
In the South China Sea, Beijing has already shored up its sovereignty claims over the past two decades by building artificial islands, often for military use. Brunei, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam dispute parts of the sea with China.
In Tokyo, which disputes a group of uninhabited islets with Beijing, the defense ministry said it had seen fighter aircraft taking off and landing from the Liaoning carrier 250 kilometers (155 miles) south of Japan’s Ishigaki Island.
The Chinese carrier group launched and recovered aircraft in Japan’s maritime exclusive economic zone during its deployment, said Colin Karotam, senior resident fellow with the Defence Strategy Program at the Australian Strategic Policy Institute. That activity is “uncommon,” Karotam said, though it may have taken place before.
The Chinese carrier group’s activities also began shortly before the Keen Sword 27 U.S.–Japan military exercises launched on Oct. 19. The exercises on Ishigaki are biennial and include the Philippines among other nations. China sees the United States, a treaty ally of both Japan and the Philippines, as a military rival in Asia.
Xinhua said the Liaoning’s movements in October comply with international law and “are not directed at any specific country or target.”

articles.title: New Zealand defense chief resigns over ‘inappropriate relationship’
articles.snippet: “These matters revolved around an inappropriate relationship I had when in a position of unit command, and I regret not disclosing this."
articles.full_text:
WELLINGTON, New Zealand — The Chief of the New Zealand Defence Force, Air Marshal Tony Davies, has informed Defense Minister Paul Goldsmith that he is resigning his role.
Arrangements are underway to transition responsibilities to the Vice Chief of Defence Force, Rear Adm. Mat Williams, who will serve as Acting Chief of Defence Force.
Air Marshal Davies said: “The resignation is for personal reasons, and results from errors of judgement made by me in the past, for which I am taking responsibility. The errors of judgement were contrary to the values of the Defence Force.
“These matters revolved around an inappropriate relationship I had when in a position of unit command, and I regret not disclosing this when I had the opportunity to do so.”
Appointed as the Chief of Air Force from 2016 before becoming the Vice Chief of Defence Force in 2018, Air Marshal Davies, born 1966, was promoted to his current rank on appointment to Chief of Defence Force on June 6, 2024.
The Chief of Army, Maj. Gen. Rose King, will act as Chief of Defence Force until Sunday before Williams takes on the role.

articles.title: Space Force reveals first 6 ‘operational’ contracts for civil reserve support in space monitoring
articles.snippet: Space Systems Command officials said the contracts are an initial step for the Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve (CASR) initiative, and don’t address the thornier issues of US rights to deny other customers service or reimbursement for satellites lost in a conflict.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — The Space Force has awarded what the service calls the first “operational” contracts under its still-nascent Commercial Augmentation Space Reserve (CASR) initiative to six space monitoring firms, Space Systems Command (SSC) announced.
The contracts are short term and designed to test military demand while the command’s Commercial Space Office (COMSO) continues to wrestle with thorny legal issues that have bedeviled the program from its launch in 2023.
The six new contracts — issued to Australian firm EOS Space Systems, Canada’s NorthStar Earth and Space, InTrack Radar, Anduril (via its acquisition of ExoAnalytic), Slingshot Aerospace, and LeoLabs — are worth a total of $1.37 million, an SSC spokesperson told Breaking Defense.
CASR is the Space Force’s planned version of the Civil Reserve Air Fleet (CRAF) for leveraging commercial airlines to support military logistics operations when needed, managed by US Transportation Command (TRANSCOM). The concept is that commercial space firms could be called upon in wartime to surge delivery of satellite-derived capabilities.
According to SSC’s Thursday press release, the contracts were let through the “General Services Administration contract framework” used by the Joint Commercial Operations cell to buy commercial data and services. Industry sources who have received similar contracts from the JCO cell have said they tend to run for no more than six months.
The new contracts follow COMSO’s March 2025 award of $1.1 million in three-month pilot contracts to four unnamed companies, first reported by Breaking Defense. Those awards were designed to test out the contracting processes and the CASR framework agreement for interested firms, rather than provide operational data.
According to reports by Air & Space Forces Magazine and Space News, COMSO head Col. Tim Tremillo told reporters during the annual Space Industry Days conference held Oct. 19-22 in Los Angeles that the initial operational awards were meant to provide a short-term boost in space domain awareness data, with the idea that these initial contracts would allow the service to judge military demand. He also made it clear that he expects the CASR program to expand both to more companies and more mission areas.
However, given the small dollar values and short contract duration of the new contracts, it is hard to see how companies will be enticed to join up, said Clayton Swope, deputy director of the Aerospace Security Project at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.
“It will be hard for companies to build capacity and capability at scale for use during a crisis if they aren’t paid to do so today. Companies otherwise will not make investments for infrastructure that sits unused and idle, ready for on-demand use, if they are not compensated to build and also maintain that surge capability. Companies do not build extra capacity for sport—it costs money,” he told Breaking Defense today.
Meanwhile, COMSO has yet to develop contractual arrangements that deal with key legal and financial issues that are critical to enticing commercial space companies to join CASR.
The first issue revolves around when and if the US government will have the right to turn off a CASR partner’s services to other customers during a conflict ― a power often referred to as “shutter control.” Companies worry that they could be accused of breach of contract by existing customers if that right were exercised by Washington, and that potential customers (particularly foreign governments) will be scared off.
The second outstanding issue is the question of whether the Pentagon will be willing to indemnify partner firms against financial losses whose satellites are damaged or destroyed during a conflict.

articles.title: Space Force shifts into high gear on cislunar warfare, with RFIs coming soon
articles.snippet: Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy, the Space Force’s portfolio acquisition executive for advanced programs, said the service wants to field cislunar capabilities by the end of fiscal 2029.
articles.full_text:
WASHINGTON — After years of sporadic experimentation, the Pentagon has embraced cislunar space as a high priority warfighting domain, pushing the Space Force to rapidly acquire commercially available technology and spacecraft, according to the service official leading the charge.
“At the beginning of the year … there was no talk of cislunar, and basically I was told: ‘Don’t talk about cislunar and stop getting into it.’ At the end of the year here, and we’re not even at the end, I’ve got the secretary of war and the chairman of the Joint Chiefs full on stating in public, ‘This is a warfighting domain’,” Maj. Gen. Stephen Purdy, Space Force portfolio acquisition executive for advanced programs, said Monday.
The Space Force plans to issue two requests for information (RFIs) in the near future seeking commercially available technology for cislunar missions and artificial intelligence software to help spacecraft operate autonomously between Earth and the Moon, Purdy said. The service wants capabilities it can field by the end of fiscal 2029.
The shift comes as senior defense officials increasingly frame cislunar space as a future battleground. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told an audience in Dayton, Ohio on Oct. 20 that “[whoever] controls subsea and cislunar is going to destroy and control the next fight.”
Purdy, who reports to Air Force Secretary Troy Meink, told the annual Space Industry Days conference in Los Angeles that the reason for the new urgency is simple: “China is moving out in this area. We have traditionally not.”
One recent Chinese project that has raised eyebrows is the launch of 30 Cubesats into a highly elliptical orbit near one of the Earth-Moon Lagrange points and a circular lunar orbit, as reported in September by the People’s Daily [Chinese language version]. While China has characterized the project at recent UN-related meetings as a science experiment, several experts told Breaking Defense it is clearly intended to support cislunar surveillance.
Purdy said research organizations such as the Air Force Research Laboratory, SpaceWERX and DARPA have been experimenting with cislunar technologies, albeit in a vacuum. Until recently, the Space Force considered cislunar space only as a potential future arena for military operations.
“They’ve been working, they’ve been passionate about this mission area, but they’ve kind of gotten no love from the broader community as we focus, perhaps rightly so, on the more terrestrial support warfighting activity,” he said.
That has changed, with senior Defense Department leaders now backing a full court press to advance US military interests in cislunar space and on the Moon. Purdy said the Office of the Secretary of Defense is launching a series of interagency policy working groups on cislunar issues. The Space Force is also working closely with NASA to coordinate infrastructure plans rather than build separate systems.
“So, yes, we’re actually attempting to build a unified architecture across the government — which should be good news to everybody — and then looking to see where [NASA is] investing and figuring out what are the deltas that we can invest in,” Purdy added.
His shop’s Cislunar Coordination Office (CCO), established in May, has been tasked with giving industry a clearer signal of the military’s needs.
“This has been a particularly onerous and bad area where we’ve really given no kind of indicator to industry, and as a result, industry hasn’t really done a whole lot into this area except what industry has been interested in,” he said.
Purdy explained that his office is not tasked to oversee all cislunar operations. Instead, it helps provide funds and support to the wider Space Force effort, while the service’s requirements and acquisition teams remain responsible for defining mission needs and procuring capabilities.
The first RFI, expected “soon,” will seek commercial technology ready for use in foundational cislunar missions, including space domain awareness and positioning, navigation and timing (PNT), Purdy said.
He cautioned that the Space Force does not want to spend buckets of research and development dollars for new capabilities; rather, the service wants working kit that can be fielded by the fourth quarter 2029.
“We want rapid deliverable capability. … I’m not going to pay you R&D funds for this stuff,” Purdy said. “We’re looking for existing commercial or near-commercial means, non-development solutions, hardware with actual relative relevant evidence behind it, software that doesn’t need a huge amount of work … and then ground systems — not as an afterthought, but as part of an integrated network.”
The second RFI, expected alongside or shortly after the first, will seek artificial intelligence software that lets spacecraft operate autonomously in the vast region between Earth and the Moon, he said. The RFI will ask industry about its capabilities in advanced AI and autonomous operations, Purdy added.
“Cislunar is a really painful space,” he explained, making autonomous operations more challenging than they are for satellites closer to the Earth. Spacecraft need to detect and manage hardware failures, process sensor data and adjust their missions as conditions change.
Meanwhile, Purdy said the CCO is refining its “nascent cislunar roadmap” that includes “mission area strategies” for things like lunar time, space domain awareness and communications.
The office also has created a list of “the emergency” unfunded requirements (UFRs) for cislunar operations, he said.
“There’s a lot of little ticky-tack things that are suffering in this area, to the tune of where a couple $100K could solve a lot of problems, which, in space terms, is like really budget dust,” he said. “But this is how bad the funding situation is, and so we now have a nice prioritized UFR list that we’re going to be able to get after. That’s real action and money and help to operators on the ground trying to glue together a couple of antennas and pull some data.”
Purdy did not disclose the total funding needed or detail the specific requirements on the list.

articles.title: FCC bans two devices with surveillance chips linked to Huawei
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The banned items — a wireless video transmitter and dashboard camera — are made with chips manufactured by Huawei subsidiary HiSilicon, which markets its products as “designed for the surveillance market.”
articles.full_text:
FCC bans two devices with surveillance chips linked to Huawei
The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) on Thursday said it won’t let devices made with surveillance chips manufactured by a Chinese tech firm enter the U.S. market, the first instance of such a ban following the agency’s implementation of tough new rules.
The banned items — a wireless video transmitter and dashboard camera — are made with chips manufactured by Huawei subsidiary HiSilicon, which markets its products as “designed for the surveillance market” with “[b]uilt in detection algorithms for human faces,” the FCC said.
New rules took effect on October 13 that bans devices containing smart components made by companies on a so-called covered list, an official public directory the agency maintains under a 2019 regulation identifying video surveillance, communications and general technology products believed to threaten national security. HiSilicon was included on the list.
Before the new regulations were implemented, agency rules did not ban “otherwise lawful devices” from including component parts manufactured by covered list entities, the press release said.
“The FCC will continue to act with vigilance in protecting and promoting America’s national security,” Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that called the products potential spyware. “Video devices containing surveillance chips produced by Covered List entities pose an obvious and unacceptable risk to the nation and our people.”
Huawei did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: UK proposes 14-year prison terms for undersea cable sabotage
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: In an era of hybrid threats, the British government wants to update the Submarine Telegraph Act 1885, which carries a maximum fine of £1,000 and five years’ imprisonment in cases of deliberate damage.
articles.full_text:
UK proposes 14-year prison terms for undersea cable sabotage
The British government proposed on Thursday introducing prison sentences of up to 14 years and unlimited fines for damaging undersea cables and pipelines.
It comes amid growing concerns over the vulnerability of subsea cables to so-called “hybrid warfare” by hostile states, including physical and cyberattacks targeting the cables themselves or the installations and digital systems on land.
According to the consultation’s white paper, the new criminal offenses would cover telecommunications cables, electricity interconnectors and pipelines carrying 99% of the U.K.’s international data traffic and supplying 74% of its gas.
The proposals would replace the Submarine Telegraph Act 1885, a Victorian-era law that carries a maximum fine of £1,000 — a fraction of the repair costs — and five years’ imprisonment in cases of deliberate damage.
Repairs to the Estlink 2 electricity cable between Finland and Estonia — damaged by the anchor of the Eagle S oil tanker on Christmas Day 2024 — were estimated by grid operator Elering at €50 million to €60 million ($56 million to $67 million). Attempts to prosecute senior officers of that ship are ongoing.
Under the new proposed law, alongside the 14 years for those found guilty of deliberate damage, perpetrators of reckless damage would face up to 10 years in prison and those of gross negligence up to two years.
The government said it plans to introduce statutory security and resilience requirements for subsea telecommunications operators, with powers to direct cable and repair providers on national security grounds. Separate rules would govern fiber-optic sensing technology, which can detect activity at sea but could expose sensitive information.
Telecoms minister Ian Murray and energy minister Michael Shanks said in a joint foreword that the risks to critical subsea infrastructure was involving, citing a warning earlier this year that a Royal Navy attack submarine had surfaced near a Russian spy ship mapping this infrastructure in British waters.
Matt Western, the chair of Parliament’s Joint Committee on the National Security Strategy, welcomed the proposals, stating “the legislation covering attacks on undersea cables was written in a different age and it is right that a White Paper has been brought forward to bring it up to date.”
Questions over jurisdiction in incidents of cable damage have complicated prosecutions elsewhere, alongside questions over whether they were truly reckless accidents or intentional attempts by Russia to undermine Europe.
Finnish investigators initially suspected deliberate damage, but officials from several North Sea and Baltic countries later told Recorded Future News they increasingly believed that incident and other Baltic Sea cable breaks were accidental, citing investigations, intelligence and shipping data.
The British government says the country’s cable network remains highly resilient and that most faults result from anchors, fishing nets, environmental hazards or technical failures while also warning of growing suspicious activity.
In April, the Ministry of Defence said British and allied forces had tracked a Russian attack submarine and vessels linked to Russia’s Main Directorate of Deep Sea Research, or GUGI, near cables and pipelines north of Britain, allegedly mapping such infrastructure for potential wartime sabotage.
The 12-week public consultation closes January 14, 2027.

articles.title: Quest Diagnostics warns of potential data theft after attack on lab service system
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Nationwide lab test company Quest Diagnostics said one of its key systems may have experienced a breach of patient data.
articles.full_text:
Quest Diagnostics warns of potential data theft after attack on lab service system
A key system used by Quest Diagnostics to manage medical test results was taken offline on Thursday after the company discovered unauthorized access.
The company published a statement and an FAQ about the cyberattack, warning customers that they “believe some patient data” within the system was accessed. The platform, Quanum Lab Services Manager (LSM), is used to place test orders as well as receive and look up results.
Access to the system has been paused while Quest investigates the attack. No other part of Quest has been impacted by the cyberattack but several other systems were paused as investigators probe the breach.
Quest said it is working with law enforcement to resolve the incident and is investigating what patient data was affected by the attack.
Customers can use paper requisitions in place of the system and Quest pledged to have Quantum back up and running by Friday. The company noted in the release that the incident did not involve the recent PHP vulnerabilities causing alarm among cybersecurity experts.
A Quest spokesperson declined to comment on the nature of the incident.
Quest is one of the largest clinical laboratory companies in the U.S., reporting more than $11 billion in revenue last year.
The New Jersey-based company says it serves half of the doctors and hospitals in the U.S. and one in three American adults each year.
No hacking group has taken credit for the incident as of Thursday afternoon. Quest is one of several healthcare testing firms to report cyber incidents in 2026. Baylor Genetics recently admitted that a data breach impacted more than 2.8 million of its patients and exposed lab results, medical testing information, Social Security numbers and more.
Several other electronic health records companies dealt with attacks this year.
In response to the attacks and several others over the last two years, Congress passed a bill this month expanding federal cyber requirements for healthcare organizations that handle patient data.

articles.title: Reports of PHP bug exploitation attempts grow as experts downplay viability of exploits
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: The headline-grabbing bugs known colloquially as PHP2Shell are giving cyber analysts a lot to track — and a lot to debunk.
articles.full_text:
Reports of PHP bug exploitation attempts grow as experts downplay viability of exploits
The two PHP vulnerabilities dominating headlines this week have left experts with a mixed bag of data to track.
Multiple large companies have reported an explosion in attempted exploitation. But dozens of experts told Recorded Future News that none of the attempts have been successful and argued that most of the available proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits only work in ideal lab conditions — making mass exploitation unlikely as of Friday.
Experts at Amazon drew headlines on Thursday with a report that they saw evidence of exploitation attempts dating back to October 17, days before news broke of CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — now known colloquially as PHP2Shell.
Sophos reported and then retracted a report of successful exploitation, writing on Thursday evening that it was only seeing a “small number of failed exploitation attempts.”
Google’s John Hultquist said his team has not validated exploitation in the wild and have no evidence of successful wide-scale exploitation, but he noted that “exploitation may have already begun in a limited fashion and the threat is viable and very serious.”
Arctic Wolf said exploitation attempts it observed were linked to the Potassium botnet, while researchers at Cobalt saw attempts tied to a Mirai botnet. Other experts similarly reported exploitation attempts that sought to infect devices with malware and turn them into bots as part of a distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) network.
Spencer McIntyre, director of exploit development at VulnCheck, said the company also has seen firsthand exploit attempts but noted that many involve PoCs that are “garbage and nonfunctional.”
The current PoCs floating around social media only work in developer and researcher environments or on production apps that do not represent how PHP is typically configured in real life, he said.
Several incident responders said those attempting to exploit the bugs are being hung up by address space layout randomization (ASLR), a protection McIntyre said was designed to make memory corruption bugs harder to exploit.
“There's a significant difference between demonstrating a vulnerability and developing an exploit that can overcome the security protections found in real-world environments,” he said.
McIntyre noted that his team has developed a novel technique to bypass ASLR but they have not identified another public or commercial exploit that does the same.
“Developing this capability was far from trivial, but it demonstrates that a major barrier to exploiting PHP2Shell on production-configured systems can be overcome,” McIntyre added.
McIntyre and other experts warned that ASLR is not a permanent barrier to exploitation of the bugs and urged organizations to patch any vulnerable systems.
What ‘exploitation’ means
Marcus Hutchins, a noted cybersecurity expert at Expel, said the difficulty of developing a reliable exploit may buy defenders a bit of time but it is impossible to predict how long it will take threat actors to come up with something viable.
In several social media posts and in comments to Recorded Future News, he argued there are two separate theories as to what companies mean when they are reporting “exploitation.”
Some are reporting sophisticated, likely state-sponsored, threat actors doing targeted exploitation while others are simply cataloging attempted mass exploitation using lab-focused PoCs that do not work.
“The second case matches the evidence I've personally seen,” Hutchins said.
While ASLR is not a “significant barrier” to successful exploitation, it does hinder attempts at mass exploitation, he added.
“Currently there are no reports that I've seen of [successful] mass exploitation, nor have I seen any mass exploitation myself. However, someone has built a scanner which can remotely identify vulnerable systems, so there are a bunch of internet-wide scan attempts ongoing,” Hutchins explained. “This means that should a fully-weaponized exploit become available, it's likely that several threat actors already have target lists containing publicly reachable unpatched systems ready to go.”
Censys created a PHP2Shell dashboard that says as of October 22, there are more than 41 million Internet-facing PHP services on affected versions and about 1 million operating with a fixed release.
Cobalt CISO Andrew Obadiaru said the lack of confirmed compromises shows how hard PHP2Shell is to weaponize but argued that the difficulty won’t last, highlighting VulnCheck’s reported exploit.
“Attackers are refining their tooling in the open, so defenders should treat this quiet period as borrowed time,” he said, warning that attackers are fingerprinting servers to find the exact configurations their exploit needs.
“Once a working technique moves from specialist tooling into botnet playbooks, defenders will have days, not weeks, to catch up.”
Jonathan Greig
is a Breaking News Reporter at Recorded Future News. Jonathan has worked across the globe as a journalist since 2014. Before moving back to New York City, he worked for news outlets in South Africa, Jordan and Cambodia. He previously covered cybersecurity at ZDNet and TechRepublic.

articles.title: Toronto crime tips org freezes operations after details of data breach come to light
articles.source: The Record from Recorded Future News
articles.snippet: Late Wednesday night the Toronto chapter of Crime Stoppers broke ranks with the national association, revealing a timeline showing what it knew and when along with an announcement that it will pause operations.
articles.full_text:
Toronto crime tips org freezes operations after details of data breach come to light
A Toronto crime prevention program that long promised witnesses a safe space to anonymously report tips froze its operations late Wednesday night, hours after a Canadian news outlet reported that more than 1.5 million tips from Crime Stoppers chapters across the country were exposed in a data breach.
Crime Stoppers urges people not to provide their names when submitting information, but reporters at Canada’s CBC broadcaster were able to reach more than a dozen tipsters by reviewing the hacked data made available to them in March by Distributed Denial of Secrets (DDoSecrets).
About half of the 1.5 million leaked tips CBC studied — some dating back 25 years — contained personal information, the outlet reported.
While Canadian Crime Stoppers Association and individual chapters, including Toronto’s, had confirmed the breach in the days after the hack, they offered no detail about what was exposed, blaming the lack of information on vendor Navigate360 and its subsidiary, P3 Global Intel.
But late Wednesday night the Toronto chapter broke ranks with the national association, revealing a timeline showing what it knew and when along with an announcement that it will pause operations.
“Since 1984, people in Toronto have come to Toronto Crime Stoppers because we promised they could stay anonymous,” Sean Sportun, chair of Toronto Crime Stoppers, said in a statement. “This week’s reporting shows that for some of them, that promise was broken. We are deeply sorry.”
The Toronto organization said it has directed Navigate360 to immediately stop taking tips and no longer process any new information. It also has told Canada’s National Anonymous Call Centre to stop receiving and processing tips meant for Toronto Crime Stoppers, according to the statement.
“Until we have a safer way to protect you, please do not send us tips by phone, online, or through the app,” the statement said.
The organization is looking for a way to take tips on a truly anonymous basis, it said.
“For more than 40 years, people in Toronto have relied on Crime Stoppers to share what they know without giving their name: a witness afraid of retaliation, a neighbour who can’t be seen talking to police, someone reporting a person close to them,” the statement said.
“Their courage has helped solve crimes, prevent tragedies, and save lives. Pausing our program means that option isn’t available now, and we did not make this decision lightly. We are pausing because those people deserve a system we can fully stand behind.”
Canadian Crime Stoppers Association and Navigate360 did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
Navigate360 told Toronto Crime Stoppers that the stolen data contained 176,859 Toronto tips, which were reported between January 2022 and November 2025, the Toronto chapter’s statement said. The vendor also told Toronto Crime Stoppers that it had found 14,973 names in those tips, but could not say if the names belonged to tipsters, suspects or both.
Toronto Crime Stoppers has made “numerous requests” through their lawyers for the text of the stolen tips, but Navigate360 has not responded, the statement said.
“Since March, Navigate360 has told us repeatedly that P3 is secure,” the statement said. “In April, it told us Toronto’s data had not been taken. When it told us in June that Toronto’s data was affected, it didn’t say what was exposed.”
A hacktivist collective known as Internet Yiff Machine took responsibility for the March breach, saying its goal was to prove that Navigate360 and P3 Global Intel lied about their capabilities.
Suzanne Smalley
is a reporter covering digital privacy, surveillance technologies and cybersecurity policy for The Record. She was previously a cybersecurity reporter at CyberScoop. Earlier in her career Suzanne covered the Boston Police Department for the Boston Globe and two presidential campaign cycles for Newsweek. She lives in Washington with her husband and three children.

articles.title: Widespread PHP Flaw May Cause Many Site Outages Today
articles.snippet: Expect to see quite a few websites serving "404" or "Page Not Found" errors today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
articles.full_text:
Expect to see quite a few websites serving error pages today: Nearly 70 percent of websites need to update their core software to fix a pair of vulnerabilities that allow an attacker to seize full control over affected servers. Experts say there are working exploits for the flaws, and that these critical bugs are already being exploited in the wild.
The flaws at issue are present in PHP, the programming language that powers sites running on a large number of web publishing systems, including Drupal, Magento, Joomla and WordPress. Earlier today, PHP released an emergency security update to fix two critical bugs that can allow an attacker to execute code of their choosing on a vulnerable server.
Reuters reports that government websites in Europe and elsewhere went offline today after the PHP vulnerabilities were disclosed. Cloudflare said it has already detected some exploitation of the flaw, and that at 3:02 am (UTC) it implemented web application firewall rules to protect websites from attack traffic seeking to exploit the bugs, which could cause a denial of service condition, remote code execution, and data exposure.
OpenAI, which was involved in the vulnerability research and outreach, said “given the severity of these flaws and PHP’s widespread use, we consider this one of the most impactful security issues in recent memory.”
Censys, a company that tracks the technology used by Internet hosts, said a recent scan identified approximately 2.58 million Internet facing hosts and 54.9 million web properties running PHP.
Security experts at Wiz said every PHP version released in the last decade is affected by at least one of these vulnerabilities [full disclosure: Wiz is an advertiser on this blog].
“These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history,” reads a blog post published today by a team of researchers at Wiz, which was one of several organizations credited with discovering the vulnerabilities. “The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit.”
The Wiz researchers say it is likely the PHP vulnerabilities will be mass-exploited to install web-based backdoors or “web shells,” which give attackers a web-based panel that allows them to remotely control infected sites. Wiz said that prior to the PHP bugs being publicly disclosed, the company worked with the PHP team, Calif and OpenAI to measure the size of the problem and coordinate patch verification and disclosure.
The PHP zero-day vulnerabilities are being tracked by their CVE numbers, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, and they affect all web servers running PHP 5.4 or later. The bugs are fixed in PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
According to Wiz, PHP is so deeply embedded in many web applications that we are likely to see organizations struggling to patch these vulnerabilities for some time to come, comparing this PHP vulnerability pair with the Log4Shell weakness that emerged in 2021 — a widespread, severe-as-it-gets security flaw in Log4j, a popular Java logging framework.
“A vulnerability in core PHP reaches far beyond a single application,” the Wiz researchers wrote. “PHP runs across clouds, hosting providers, content-delivery networks and millions of independently managed servers. Reducing exposure before the technical details became public required coordinated work across that entire ecosystem.”
The SANS Internet Storm Center is keeping an eye on major software platforms that are shipping updates to deal with these PHP flaws. For example, Ubuntu just released updated PHP packages. For a technical deep-dive on these vulnerabilities that tells the timeline of the discovery of these bugs in a comic book style, check out this post from Calif, another technology company credited with finding the PHP flaws.
This is a fast-moving story. Updates will be noted here with timestamps.
Update, 2:30 pm ET: Add figures from Censys and a link to Calif’s writeup.
